claims.section: Abstract
claims.label: Self-assembly emerges from cells sharing a common model of organismal form
claims.claim: In simulations based on variational free-energy minimization (active inference), cells that share a common genetically and epigenetically specified model of the organism's form self-assemble into that form, offering a proof of principle that self-assembly can be an emergent property of such cells.
claims.quote: Here, we offer a proof of principle that self-assembly is an emergent property of cells that share a common (genetic and epigenetic) model of organismal form.
claims.scope: Active-inference simulation of eight cells forming a head–body–tail morphology
measurable_quantities: final cell positions and identities versus target morphology
ensemble free energy over time
claims.candidate_data: SPM software (spm_ADEM.m) for reproducing the simulation; none known for empirical data.

claims.section: Abstract
claims.label: Genome parametrizes a generative model; epigenesis inverts it
claims.claim: Under the free-energy account of morphogenesis, genetic codes can be interpreted as parametrizing a generative model that predicts the signals each cell would sense in the target morphology, and epigenetic processes (signalling-dependent transcription) as the inversion of that model.
claims.quote: This novel perspective on the coordination of migration and differentiation of cells suggests an interpretation of genetic codes as parametrizing a generative model—predicting the signals sensed by cells in the target morphology—and epigenetic processes as the subsequent inversion of that model.
claims.scope: Morphogenesis in multicellular organisms
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.section: Introduction
claims.label: Morphogenesis requires each cell to model its place in the target form
claims.claim: Friston, Levin, Sengupta and Pezzulo propose that morphogenetic self-organization requires each cell to have an implicit model of its place in the final morphology, with self-assembly being cells moving to sample the local signals that model predicts (minimizing variational free energy).
claims.quote: In this paper, we pursue the notion that morphogenetic self-organization requires each cell to have an implicit model of its place in the final morphology [21]—and that self-assembly is the process of moving to sample local signals that are predicted by that model.
claims.scope: Cells during embryogenesis and regeneration
measurable_quantities: cell migration trajectories relative to signal gradients
signal concentrations sensed at final positions
claims.candidate_data: Live-imaging cell-tracking datasets of embryogenesis (e.g. in the Image Data Resource or Cell Tracking Challenge).

claims.section: Introduction
claims.label: Free energy is minimized only when every cell occupies a unique inferred place
claims.claim: In the active-inference model of morphogenesis, where identical pluripotent cells share one generative model, the minimum of variational free energy is reached only when every cell is at a unique location and has correctly inferred its place, so free-energy minimization guarantees convergence to the target form.
claims.quote: This is guaranteed because the minimum of variational free energy is obtained when each cell is in a unique location and has correctly inferred its place.
claims.scope: Active-inference model of morphogenesis with cells sharing a generative model
measurable_quantities: ensemble free energy
uniqueness of cell identity assignments
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.section: Simulating self-assembly
claims.label: Simulated cells resolve fate ambiguity using context set by other ambiguous cells
claims.claim: In the active-inference simulation, identical undifferentiated cells starting at one location migrate rapidly to their target locations and then differentiate (around the eighth time step) into head, body and tail types as ensemble free energy falls, showing cells can resolve ambiguity about their fate even when it depends on context set by other equally ambiguous cells.
claims.quote: These results are compelling in the sense that they show cells can resolve ambiguity about their fate, even when that resolution depends upon the context established by other (equally ambiguous) cells.
claims.scope: Active-inference simulation of eight cells forming a head–body–tail morphology
measurable_quantities: cell identity confusion matrix over time
time to migration and differentiation
claims.candidate_data: SPM software (spm_ADEM.m) for reproducing the simulation.

claims.section: Simulating regeneration and dysmorphogenesis
claims.label: Bisected simulated embryos regenerate the full target form
claims.claim: When the partially differentiated simulated embryo is cut in two and each half's cells are replicated, the cells undergo slight dedifferentiation and then each half regenerates the complete head–body–tail target morphology, illustrating pluripotency and recovery from drastic interventions in the active-inference model.
claims.quote: This example illustrates the pluripotential nature of the cells and the ability of self-assembly to recover from fairly drastic interventions.
claims.scope: Active-inference morphogenesis simulation (analogous to planarian or regulative embryo bisection)
measurable_quantities: morphology of each half after continued simulation
degree of dedifferentiation
claims.candidate_data: SPM software for the simulation; planarian regeneration data (e.g. PlanMine) for comparison.

claims.section: Simulating regeneration and dysmorphogenesis
claims.label: Altering signal sensitivity without changing the model predicts specific birth defects
claims.claim: In the active-inference morphogenesis model, changing cells' sensitivity to extracellular, exogenous or intracellular signals without changing the generative model produces specific dysmorphogenesis, e.g. reducing sensitivity to the head-expressed signal shrinks the head, and doubling sensitivity to intracellular signals causes failed migration, differentiation and atrophy; these are predictions for pharmacological manipulation of intercellular signalling.
claims.quote: More selective interventions produce a dysmorphogenesis of various segments of the target morphology: reducing sensitivity to the second chemotactic signal—that is expressed by head cells—reduces the size of the head.
claims.scope: Active-inference morphogenesis simulation; proposed for real embryos under signalling perturbation
measurable_quantities: size of body segments after altered signal-receptor sensitivity
differentiation of cell types
claims.candidate_data: Teratogen and receptor-inhibitor phenotype data in model-organism databases such as ZFIN and Xenbase.

claims.section: Conclusion
claims.label: Neural and bioelectric patterning networks may share dynamics
claims.claim: Because non-neuronal cells use many of the same ion-channel and electrical-synapse mechanisms as neurons for pattern formation and repair, significant commonalities may exist between the dynamics of neural networks and of bioelectric signalling networks that control shape, so neural modelling tools such as dynamic causal modelling may apply to morphogenesis data.
claims.quote: This suggests the possibility that significant commonalities may exist between the dynamics of neural networks and of bioelectric signalling networks that control shape determination [20,21,83].
claims.scope: Non-neural tissues with bioelectric signalling during development and regeneration
measurable_quantities: ion-channel and gap-junction expression in non-neural patterning tissues
fit of dynamic causal models to bioelectric time-series
claims.candidate_data: Ion-channel expression in developing tissues (Xenbase, Gene Expression Omnibus); voltage-dye imaging data in the Image Data Resource where available.

claims.section: Conclusion
claims.label: An exogenous gradient makes self-assembly more robust for larger ensembles
claims.claim: In the active-inference morphogenesis simulations, an exogenous concentration gradient is not necessary but yields a more robust solution for larger ensembles (more than four clones) and fixes the orientation of the target morphology relative to an external frame of reference.
claims.quote: This is not a necessary component of the scheme; however, our simulations suggest that it underwrites a more robust solution for larger ensembles (with more than four clones).
claims.scope: Active-inference morphogenesis simulation
measurable_quantities: accuracy of final morphology with and without exogenous gradient as ensemble size varies
claims.candidate_data: SPM software (spm_ADEM.m) for reproducing the simulation.

claims.section: Conclusion
claims.label: Epigenetic active inference is indispensable for patterning beyond genetic encoding
claims.claim: Although aspects of the target morphology are genetically encoded in the parameters of cells' generative models, epigenetic processes (active inference) are indispensable for patterning, consistent with the regenerative target morphology of planaria being permanently alterable (to two heads) by a brief modification of electric synapses.
claims.quote: It may be worth concluding that although aspects of the target morphology are genetically encoded (in the parameters of the generative models); epigenetic processes (active inference) are indispensable for patterning.
claims.scope: Morphogenesis and regeneration, e.g. planarian regeneration
measurable_quantities: persistence of altered target morphology without genetic change
claims.candidate_data: Published planarian gap-junction-blockade regeneration data; PlanMine.

claims.section: Abstract
claims.label: Brief gap-junction blockade makes G. dorotocephala regenerate other species' head shapes
claims.claim: In decapitated Girardia dorotocephala fragments, a transient perturbation of cell-to-cell physiological connectivity with the gap junction blocker octanol can lead to regenerated heads whose shapes stochastically match those of other planarian species (Schmidtea mediterranea, Dugesia japonica, Polycelis felina).
claims.quote: after decapitation in G. dorotocephala, a transient perturbation of physiological connectivity among cells (using the gap junction blocker octanol) can result in regenerated heads with quite different shapes, stochastically matching other known species of planaria (S. mediterranea, D. japonica, and P. felina)
claims.scope: Regenerating pre-tail fragments of genetically wild-type Girardia dorotocephala treated with octanol (123 µM, 3 days)
measurable_quantities: head shape class of regenerates
fraction of regenerates per head-shape class
octanol dose and exposure duration
claims.candidate_data: New planarian regeneration experiments with gap junction blockers and head-shape imaging; planarian resources such as PlanMine for cross-species comparison.

claims.section: 2. Results › 2.2. Quantitative Comparison of Induced vs. Genome-Specific Head Shapes
claims.label: Octanol-induced head shapes are morphometrically closer to the species they resemble
claims.claim: By geometric morphometrics (Procrustes distances), the octanol-induced head shapes of G. dorotocephala regenerates are closer to the wild-type head shapes of the species they resemble than to the wild-type G. dorotocephala head shape.
claims.quote: Comparisons of the Procrustes distances between shape groups (Figure 2A, Table 1) showed that the experimentally derived morphologies were closer in shape to the wild-type morphologies they resembled than the wild-type Girardia dorotocephala head morphology.
claims.scope: Landmark-based head shapes of octanol-treated G. dorotocephala regenerates and wild-type G. dorotocephala, D. japonica, S. mediterranea and P. felina
measurable_quantities: Procrustes distances between head-shape groups
canonical variate scores
centroid size
claims.candidate_data: Head images of wild-type planarian species from museum or lab collections and new images of treated regenerates, analysed with standard geometric morphometrics.

claims.section: 2. Results › 2.3. The Head Shape Changes Are Stochastic
claims.label: Induced head shapes are stochastic, with frequencies tracking evolutionary distance
claims.claim: Under identical octanol treatment, G. dorotocephala regenerates take one of several discrete head shapes, and the frequencies of the shapes are unequal and correlate roughly with the evolutionary distance (from rRNA phylogeny) between G. dorotocephala and the species each shape resembles, with shapes of closer relatives (S. mediterranea, D. japonica) more frequent than that of the more distant P. felina.
claims.quote: We conclude that not only are phenotypic outcomes from physiological network perturbation stochastic (as the same treatment leads to one of several discrete shapes among individuals), but the frequencies are not equal and correlate roughly with evolutionary distance between the worm species these heads resemble.
claims.scope: Octanol-treated G. dorotocephala regenerates; four planarian species placed on an rRNA-based tree
measurable_quantities: frequency of each pseudo-species head shape
phylogenetic distance between planarian species
claims.candidate_data: Planarian rRNA and transcriptome sequences in GenBank and PlanMine for phylogenetic distances, plus new counts of induced head-shape frequencies.

claims.section: 2. Results › 2.4. Brain Structure of GJ-Perturbed Worms Is Also Altered to That of Other Species
claims.label: Gap-junction-perturbed worms also acquire the brain shape of the species they resemble
claims.claim: G. dorotocephala regenerates whose heads resemble another species after octanol treatment also have brain morphologies (length/width ratio, by anti-synapsin staining) resembling the brains of wild-type worms of that species.
claims.quote: Strikingly, we found that pseudo worms possessed brain morphologies that look like the brain morphologies of wild-type worms whose head shapes they resembled (Figure 4D–F) (ANOVA, p < 0.001).
claims.scope: Octanol-treated G. dorotocephala regenerates compared with wild-type G. dorotocephala, D. japonica and S. mediterranea
measurable_quantities: brain length/width ratio
head shape class
claims.candidate_data: Planarian nervous-system immunostaining images (e.g., in the Cell Image Library or new experiments) across species and after treatment.

claims.section: 2. Results › 2.5. Distribution of Neoblasts Is Altered to That of Other Species in GJ-Perturbed Worms
claims.label: Perturbed worms adopt the anterior stem-cell distribution of the species they resemble
claims.claim: In octanol-treated G. dorotocephala regenerates, the transformation toward another species' head shape extends to the species-characteristic distribution of neoblasts (mitotic stem cells) in the anterior body, and the authors conclude that the patterning processes disrupted by gap junction perturbation also organize the distribution of mitotically active cells.
claims.quote: We conclude that the transformation of G. dorotocephala worms to resemble other species also extends to the species-specific, characteristic internal distribution of their stem cells, and that the patterning processes that are disrupted after GJC perturbation are also responsible for organizing the distribution of mitotically active cells.
claims.scope: Phospho-histone H3-positive neoblasts in the anterior sixth of octanol-treated G. dorotocephala and wild-type G. dorotocephala, D. japonica and S. mediterranea
measurable_quantities: number of H3P-positive cells in the anterior sixth of the body
head shape class
claims.candidate_data: Planarian neoblast single-cell and marker data in PlanMine and the Gene Expression Omnibus, plus new H3P staining across species and treatments.

claims.section: 2. Results › 2.6. Patterns of Endogenous Relative Membrane Potential Are Altered in GJ-Perturbed Worms
claims.label: Octanol-treated worms show more isopotential regions, which return to normal by 30 days
claims.claim: Ten days after transient octanol exposure, regenerated G. dorotocephala show more distinct isopotential (membrane-voltage) regions by DiBAC dye imaging than controls, and the number of isopotential regions returns to the wild-type level after 30 days of morphological remodeling.
claims.quote: We detected an increased number of isopotential regions in the pseudo worms compared to the states of control worms; interestingly, the numbers of isopotential regions return to those of a wild-type state after 30 days of morphological remodeling (Figure 6I).
claims.scope: Whole-body DiBAC4(3) voltage-dye images of octanol-treated and control G. dorotocephala at 10 and 30 days
measurable_quantities: number of distinct isopotential regions per worm
relative membrane potential (DiBAC fluorescence)
days after treatment
claims.candidate_data: New voltage-dye imaging of planarians; no public planarian bioelectric imaging dataset is known.

claims.section: 2. Results › 2.7. Induced Shape Changes Are Not Permanent
claims.label: Induced head shapes remodel back toward G. dorotocephala after regeneration ends
claims.claim: The other-species head shapes induced in G. dorotocephala by octanol are not permanent: between days 10 and 30, after regeneration is complete and without further injury, the heads are remodeled to more closely resemble wild-type G. dorotocephala.
claims.quote: We found that the induced morphologies were remodeled, long after regenerative processes had ended, to produce morphologies that bore closer resemblance to wild-type G. dorotocephala.
claims.scope: Octanol-induced pseudo-species G. dorotocephala photographed daily from day 10 to day 30
measurable_quantities: head shape over time after regeneration
time to return to wild-type shape
claims.candidate_data: New time-lapse imaging of treated planarians with morphometric scoring.

claims.section: 2. Results › 2.7. Induced Shape Changes Are Not Permanent
claims.label: Head remodeling passes from S. mediterranea-like to D. japonica-like to normal shape
claims.claim: In canonical variate shape space, the D. japonica head morphology lies between those of G. dorotocephala and S. mediterranea, and octanol-induced S. mediterranea-like G. dorotocephala heads remodel by moving from S. mediterranea-like to D. japonica-like to G. dorotocephala morphology.
claims.quote: DJ morphology lies between GD and SM morphologies in this space, and we observe remodeling that moves from SM morphology to DJ morphology to GD morphology.
claims.scope: Remodeling octanol-treated G. dorotocephala regenerates, days 10–30
measurable_quantities: canonical variate scores of head shape over time
claims.candidate_data: New longitudinal morphometric data of remodeling planarians alongside wild-type species head images.

claims.section: 2. Results › 2.8. A Model of Planarian Head Shapes Arising from Cell Interactions
claims.label: Agent-based model of migrating, signaling cells reproduces the observed head shapes
claims.claim: In an agent-based model of planarian head regeneration in which static somatic cells emit a chemical signal and migratory cells (neoblasts or their progeny) are repelled by it, deactivating different subsets of signaling cells (representing octanol gap-junction blockade) reproduces the four observed head shapes, so a small set of gap-junction-regulated cell behaviors such as migration and cell-cell signaling can quantitatively explain the observed morphologies.
claims.quote: We conclude that a small set of cell-level behaviors, such as migration and cell-cell signaling that are known to be regulated by GJC and thus are perturbed by octanol exposure [35,39,49,98,101,102], can quantitatively explain the morphologies we observed in planaria.
claims.scope: The authors' two-cell-type agent-based model of the planarian head with an elastic boundary
measurable_quantities: simulated head length and width intervals (L1, L2)
measured head dimensions of real worms
claims.candidate_data: The paper's model description in its supplementary material; new morphometric data from planarians for comparison.

claims.section: 3. Discussion › 3.1. Perturbation of Bioelectric Networks Produces Inter-Species Morphological Change
claims.label: Coherent discrete head shapes show the octanol effect is instructive rather than toxic
claims.claim: The octanol-induced head-shape change in G. dorotocephala is instructive rather than a toxic or housekeeping defect, because it yields one of several coherent, ecologically valid morphologies rather than regeneration failure or disorganized growth, with no intermediate morphologies observed.
claims.quote: The head morphology alteration effect was instructive, and not merely one of toxicity or a house-keeping defect, because the outcome was not merely disruption of regenerative ability or a generalized mis-patterning (e.g., tumor or other disorganized growth), but rather resulted in one of several coherent (and ecologically-valid) morphologies.
claims.scope: Octanol-treated G. dorotocephala regenerates
measurable_quantities: fraction of regenerates with coherent species-like shapes versus intermediate or disorganized shapes
claims.candidate_data: New morphometric data on treated regenerates testing for intermediate shapes.

claims.section: 3. Discussion › 3.1. Perturbation of Bioelectric Networks Produces Inter-Species Morphological Change
claims.label: Hexanol, which does not block gap junctions, does not alter head shape
claims.claim: In G. dorotocephala, the same 3-day exposure to hexanol, a closely related alcohol that does not efficiently block gap junction channels, does not produce altered head morphologies, consistent with the head-shape change depending on octanol's gap-junction-blocking activity rather than a generalized effect of long-chain alcohols.
claims.quote: The same 3-day treatment with the closely related alcohol, hexanol (6-OH), which does not efficiently block gap junction channels, and subsequent regeneration in water for 7 days, did not produce altered morphologies, consistent with the importance of the GJ-blocking activity of octanol, and not some other generalized effect of long-chain alcohols.
claims.scope: Regenerating G. dorotocephala fragments treated with hexanol versus octanol
measurable_quantities: incidence of altered head morphologies after hexanol versus octanol exposure
gap junction coupling under each alcohol
claims.candidate_data: New planarian regeneration experiments comparing alcohols, ideally with dye-coupling assays of gap junction function.

claims.section: 3. Discussion › 3.1. Perturbation of Bioelectric Networks Produces Inter-Species Morphological Change
claims.label: Bioelectric networks derive distinct morphologies from one genome
claims.claim: Physiological bioelectric networks are a previously unrecognized input by which distinct morphologies, including those of other species, can be derived from the same genome, as shown by gap-junction perturbation in G. dorotocephala.
claims.quote: Here, we identify a novel physiological input into the process by which distinct morphologies can be derived from the same genome: physiological bioelectric networks.
claims.scope: Planarian head regeneration (G. dorotocephala), proposed as a general input to morphogenesis
measurable_quantities: morphological outcome under bioelectric perturbation in isogenic animals
genomic sequence identity between treated and control animals
claims.candidate_data: Planarian genome and transcriptome resources (PlanMine, SmedGD) to confirm genetic identity, combined with new bioelectric perturbation experiments.

claims.section: 3. Discussion › 3.4. Bioelectric State of Tissues and Its Stable Alteration in Species-Specific Shape Change
claims.label: Brief gap-junction blockade persistently alters bioelectric state after drug washout
claims.claim: In G. dorotocephala, the long-lasting alteration of bioelectric patterning after brief octanol exposure is not caused by residual octanol (which leaves tissues within 24 h) but is initiated by octanol's disruption of gap junction communication, which alters bioelectric network topology and results in a persistent perturbation of bioelectric state.
claims.quote: Although these long-lasting alterations in bioelectrical patterning are not directly caused by octanol remaining within the body of the worm (since 8-OH is known to depart planarian tissues within 24 h [20]), they are initiated by the octanol-mediated disruption of GJC, which alters bioelectric network topology, and results in persistent perturbation of bioelectric state.
claims.scope: G. dorotocephala somatic tissues after transient octanol exposure
measurable_quantities: tissue octanol concentration over time
gap junction coupling (dye transfer) over time
isopotential region count
claims.candidate_data: New GC-MS washout measurements combined with time-course dye-coupling and voltage imaging in planarians.

claims.section: 3. Discussion › 3.4. Bioelectric State of Tissues and Its Stable Alteration in Species-Specific Shape Change
claims.label: Partial, variable gap-junction blockade is consistent with stochastic head-shape outcomes
claims.claim: The variability and overall magnitude of the bioelectric effect imply that octanol only partially shuts down gap junction communication in each G. dorotocephala (affecting some percentage of gap junctions per animal), which the authors consider consistent with the stochasticity of the head-shape phenotype.
claims.quote: The variability and overall magnitude of the effect imply that the result of 8-OH exposure is only partially effective in shutting down GJC (affecting some percentage of GJs in any animal); this is consistent with the stochasticity of the morphological phenotype (Figure 3).
claims.scope: Octanol-treated G. dorotocephala
measurable_quantities: fraction of gap junctions blocked per animal
inter-animal variability of coupling
head-shape outcome per animal
claims.candidate_data: New per-animal coupling measurements paired with head-shape scoring; none known publicly.

claims.section: 3. Discussion › 3.4. Bioelectric State of Tissues and Its Stable Alteration in Species-Specific Shape Change
claims.label: Head shape may be encoded in time-dependent rather than steady voltage patterns
claims.claim: Because single-image voltage distributions showed no simple correspondence with the head shapes of octanol-treated G. dorotocephala, the authors consider it most likely that shape outcomes are encoded in time-dependent bioelectric activity rather than in steady voltage distributions, as in information encoding in the central nervous system.
claims.quote: The most likely explanation however is that shape outcomes may not be encoded via steady (single-image) distributions but in time-dependent activity, as occurs during information encoding in the central nervous system.
claims.scope: Planarian bioelectric patterns and head-shape outcomes
measurable_quantities: time series of membrane voltage across planarian tissue
head shape outcome
claims.candidate_data: New voltage-imaging movies of regenerating planarians; none known publicly.

claims.section: 3. Discussion › 3.5. Morphological Remodeling in 2 Phases: Head Shape Change without Traumatic Injury
claims.label: Planarian morphology behaves as a homeostatic parameter maintained toward a target shape
claims.claim: In planarians, morphology appears to be a homeostatic parameter that is repeatedly assessed and adjusted to maintain a 'target' morphology: after an incorrect head shape is produced during regeneration, the mismatch with the target triggers remodeling (between days 10 and 17 in octanol-treated G. dorotocephala), even after large-scale reorganization has ended.
claims.quote: Morphology appears to be a homeostatic parameter, one that is consistently assessed and adjusted in order to maintain some “target” morphology.
claims.scope: Regenerating and remodeling planarians (G. dorotocephala)
measurable_quantities: onset time of remodeling
deviation of head shape from species-typical shape over time
claims.candidate_data: Time-course planarian imaging and morphometrics; none known publicly.

claims.section: 3. Discussion › 3.6. Computational Modeling of Head Shape Formation
claims.label: Gap-junction-dependent instructive signals pass from somatic tissue to neoblasts
claims.claim: The authors propose that significant instructive, gap-junction-dependent signaling passes from planarian somatic tissues to neoblasts or their progeny to guide new tissue generation and shaping during regeneration.
claims.quote: In this model, we propose that significant instructive (GJ-dependent) signaling occurs from the somatic tissues to the neoblasts or their progeny, to guide the new tissue generation and shaping during regeneration.
claims.scope: Regenerating planarian heads
measurable_quantities: innexin expression in somatic cells versus neoblasts
neoblast migration paths after cell-type-specific gap junction knockdown
claims.candidate_data: Planarian single-cell atlases in PlanMine and the Gene Expression Omnibus for innexin expression by cell type; new cell-type-specific RNAi experiments.

claims.section: 3. Discussion › 3.7. A hypothesis: Physiological Network Attractors Underlie Regions of Anatomical Morphospace
claims.label: Somatic cells can be modeled as a slow neural-like network obeying brain-like dynamics
claims.claim: The authors propose conceptualizing the link between gap junctional connectivity among planarian cells and discrete regenerative outcomes by viewing the cells as a neural-like network that processes developmental information more slowly but obeys the same statistical dynamics as the brain.
claims.quote: Thus, we propose that one way to conceptualize the linkage between bioelectrical connectivity among worm cells (GJC) and discrete global behavioral outcomes achieved by regeneration is to view the worms’ cells as a neural-like network, processing developmental information more slowly but obeying the same statistical dynamics rules as are known to occur in the brain (Figure 9A).
claims.scope: Planarian somatic cell networks during regeneration
claims.candidate_data: None known.

claims.section: 3. Discussion › 3.7. A hypothesis: Physiological Network Attractors Underlie Regions of Anatomical Morphospace
claims.label: Planarian head shapes may be attractors of a gap-junction-coupled bioelectric network
claims.claim: The authors hypothesize that distinct planarian head shapes may be attractors in the state space of the bioelectric network formed by body cells coupled by gap junctions, that these attractors correspond to regions of morphospace in the evolutionary sense, and that octanol knocks the network's stochastic dynamics into one of several nearby attractors normally belonging to other flatworm species.
claims.quote: We hypothesize that distinct shape outcomes may be attractors in a state space describing distinct modes of the bioelectric network of planarian body cells connected by gap junctions (electrical synapses); in essence, these attractors correspond to regions of a morphospace as classically understood by evolutionary theory [151].
claims.scope: Planarian body-wide bioelectric networks (G. dorotocephala and related species)
measurable_quantities: multistability of simulated or measured bioelectric network states
mapping of network states to head shapes
claims.candidate_data: None known; would require new bioelectric network models and cell-resolution voltage time series.

claims.section: 3. Discussion › 3.7. A hypothesis: Physiological Network Attractors Underlie Regions of Anatomical Morphospace
claims.label: Regeneration as descent to a free-energy attractor; induced shapes as local minima
claims.claim: On the authors' proposed view, discrete planarian head patterns are the lowest free-energy outcomes of bioelectric network dynamics; amputation raises free energy and regeneration is a return to a low-energy attractor, octanol shifts the system to another attractor, and the induced other-species shapes are only local minima since worms return to the global minimum of G. dorotocephala morphology after about 3–4 weeks.
claims.quote: On this view (Figure 9), the discrete head patterns are outcomes of bioelectric network dynamics with the lowest free-energy; cutting the network raises the free energy by deviating the system from its optimal morphology (damage), and initiates the regenerative process—a journey back down to a low-energy attractor.
claims.scope: Planarian regeneration conceived as dynamics of a bioelectric network
claims.candidate_data: None known.

claims.section: 3. Discussion › 3.8. Stochastic Phenotypes and Evolutionary Implications
claims.label: Planarian evolutionary distance may reflect ease of shifting a shared patterning network
claims.claim: The authors suggest that a core network of gene-regulatory elements and gap-junction-mediated signals may be shared among many planarians, with species differences tweaking its dynamics, so that evolutionary distance between planarian species may reflect how easily this network can be shifted into its different outcome states, as during gap junction inhibition.
claims.quote: The evolutionary distance among the planarian types may thus be expected to reflect the ease of shifting this network into its different potential outcome states (as occurs during GJC inhibition).
claims.scope: Planarian species (Girardia, Dugesia, Schmidtea, Polycelis/Phagocata)
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic distance between species
frequency with which perturbation of one species yields another's morphology
claims.candidate_data: Planarian phylogenies from GenBank sequences and PlanMine transcriptomes, combined with new perturbation experiments across several species.

claims.section: Abstract
claims.label: Resting potential of distant cells controls oncogene-dependent tumorigenesis
claims.claim: The resting membrane potentials of cells located at a distance from oncogene-expressing cells are critical for whether those oncogene-expressing cells go on to form tumors in vivo, as shown in Xenopus laevis tadpoles injected with human oncogenes.
claims.quote: Extending prior work focused on the bioelectric state of cancer cells themselves, we show for the first time that the resting potentials of distant cells are critical for oncogene-dependent tumorigenesis.
claims.scope: Xenopus laevis embryos/tadpoles injected with human or Xenopus oncogene mRNAs (Xrel3, Gli1, KRASG12D)
measurable_quantities: resting membrane potential (Vmem) of cells remote from the oncogene-injected site
incidence of induced tumor-like structures per embryo
distance between hyperpolarized and oncogene-expressing regions
claims.candidate_data: Xenopus voltage-reporter dye imaging and tumor-incidence scoring datasets, Xenbase gene expression and phenotype records for ion channels and oncogenes, and image repositories such as the Image Data Resource or the Cell Image Library.

claims.section: Abstract
claims.label: Oncogene-induced tumor-like structures in Xenopus share hallmarks of human tumors
claims.claim: Tumor-like structures induced in Xenopus laevis tadpoles by human oncogenes such as mutant KRAS display overproliferation, increased nuclear size, hypoxia, intracellular acidity and leukocyte attraction, hallmarks shared with classic human tumors.
claims.quote: In the Xenopus laevis tadpole model, we used human oncogenes such as mutant KRAS to drive formation of tumor-like structures that exhibited overproliferation, increased nuclear size, hypoxia, acidity, and leukocyte attraction.
claims.scope: Induced tumor-like structures (ITLS) in Xenopus laevis embryos injected with Xrel3, Gli1 or KRASG12D mRNA
measurable_quantities: fraction of cells in G2/S/M phase (FUCCI reporter)
pimonidazole hypoxia staining intensity
nuclear cross-sectional area
intracellular pH
leukocyte density at the tumor site

claims.section: RESULTS › Long-range hyperpolarization suppresses the formation of ITLS
