phylogenetic order of appearance of developmental versus neural uses
claims.candidate_data: Comparative genomics of ion channels and innexins/connexins across early-branching animals (UniProt, InterPro) and developmental expression atlases.

claims.section: Body Patterning and Cognition: A Common Origin
claims.label: Brain cognition lies on a continuum with conserved pre-neural computation
claims.claim: Given the deep evolutionary conservation of ion-channel and neurotransmitter mechanisms between developmental and behavioural processes, the cognitive capacities of advanced brains are likely on a continuum with, and evolved from, much simpler computational processes conserved at both the functional and molecular levels.
claims.quote: Thus, it is likely that the cognitive capacities of advanced brains lie on a continuum with, and evolve from, much simpler computational processes that are widely conserved at both the functional and mechanism (molecular) levels.
claims.scope: Nervous systems and their pre-neural cellular precursors across the tree of life
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic distribution of ion channel and neurotransmitter pathway genes
presence of learning or memory behaviours in aneural organisms
claims.candidate_data: Comparative genomics and protein-family resources (UniProt, InterPro, OrthoDB) for ion channel and neurotransmitter gene distribution, plus published basal-cognition behavioural assays.

claims.section: Multicellularity vs. Cancer: The Shifting Boundary of the Self
claims.label: Disrupting or restoring cell communication should trigger or suppress cancer
claims.claim: The shrinking-Self view of cancer predicts that interfering with physiological communication among cells should be able to trigger cancer and restoring it should suppress cancer, and that the relevant parameter (communication) is spread over considerable distance rather than confined to single cells as genomic damage is.
claims.quote: This view predicts that interference with (or restoration of) physiological communication among cells should be able to trigger (or suppress) cancer and that the relevant parameter (communication) is spread out over considerable distance and not confined to single cells (e.g., genomic damage).
claims.scope: Metazoan tissues; tested so far in amphibian models
measurable_quantities: tumour incidence after gap junction blockade
tumour incidence after restoring coupling or membrane potential
spatial range of the cells whose state affects tumour formation
claims.candidate_data: Published Xenopus tumour and depolarization experiments, carcinogenicity data on gap junction blockers, and cancer expression data in the Gene Expression Omnibus.

claims.section: Multicellularity vs. Cancer: The Shifting Boundary of the Self
claims.label: Depolarization induces and hyperpolarization prevents tumour-like changes in tadpoles
claims.claim: In tadpoles, depolarizing a specific cell population is sufficient to cause metastatic-like transformation of normal melanocytes in genetically normal animals, while optogenetic or constitutive hyperpolarization prevents human oncogenes from inducing tumours.
claims.quote: metastatic transformation of normal melanocytes can be achieved in genetically normal tadpoles simply by depolarizing a specific cell population (Lobikin et al., 2012), while, conversely, human oncogenes which normally induce tumors can be prevented from doing so simply by optogenetic or constitutive hyperpolarization (Chernet and Levin, 2013b, 2014; Chernet et al., 2015, 2016).
claims.scope: Xenopus laevis tadpoles; melanocytes and human-oncogene-induced tumours
measurable_quantities: resting membrane potential of target cells
fraction of animals with melanocyte hyperpigmentation and invasion
tumour incidence with and without hyperpolarization
claims.candidate_data: The cited Levin-lab Xenopus studies' published counts and imaging; Xenbase for gene and reagent information.

claims.section: Multicellularity vs. Cancer: The Shifting Boundary of the Self
claims.label: Cancer cells are no more selfish than normal cells; their self is smaller
claims.claim: Cells in a metazoan body are not less selfish than unicellular organisms or cancer cells; all are equally selfish, but the self that normal somatic cells defend is larger in space, time and complexity, its boundary being set by how far information passes between subunits.
claims.quote: They are equally selfish, working only for the benefit of themselves, but the relevant self that they defend is bigger in terms of space, time, and complexity. As will be argued below, what defines this Self is the boundary of information being able to pass between the subunits.
claims.scope: Somatic metazoan cells, cancer cells and unicellular organisms
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.section: Multicellularity vs. Cancer: The Shifting Boundary of the Self
claims.label: Most biological systems consist of multiple nested selves
claims.claim: Under Scale-Free Cognition, most biological systems consist of multiple, nested selves rather than one, each inner agent maintaining its own Self only to the extent that it restricts information flow from its neighbours.
claims.quote: It is an essential aspect of Scale-Free Cognition that most biological systems consist of multiple, nested selves [not one, as implied by Integrated Information Theory (Tononi, 2008)].
claims.scope: Multilevel biological systems (molecular networks, cells, tissues, organs, organisms, swarms)
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.section: Defining Individuation From a Cognitive Perspective
claims.label: An Individual is defined by the scale and types of goals it can pursue
claims.claim: The scale and types of goals (in the cybernetic sense of feedback toward a specific state) that a system can pursue define the boundaries and content of that system as an agent or Individual; the coherent Self is the set of parts that operate together toward specific goal states.
claims.quote: I propose a definition of an Individual based on its information-processing structure (Barandiaran et al., 2009): the scale and types of goals that a system can pursue defines (determines) the boundaries and content of the putative “agent.”
claims.scope: Biological individuals at any level of organization, plus artificial and exobiological agents
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.section: Defining Individuation From a Cognitive Perspective
claims.label: Cognitive light cones have expanded over evolutionary time
claims.claim: The volume of possible cognitive light cones (spatio-temporal boundaries of agents' goals) has presumably kept expanding over evolutionary time, through innovations in body structure that drastically enlarge the cognitive boundary, although some lineages contract it permanently or in particular life stages.
claims.quote: Presumably, the volume of possible cognitive light cones keeps expanding with evolutionary time (although some lineages can contract it, permanently or during specific ontogenetic life stages). Over evolutionary scales, there have been “inflationary leaps” – innovations in body structure which drastically increase the cognitive boundary of viable selves.
claims.scope: Evolution of agents across the tree of life
measurable_quantities: estimated spatial and temporal range of sensing, memory and anticipation per lineage over geological time
claims.candidate_data: Comparative behavioural and memory-span data across taxa combined with dated phylogenies (e.g. TimeTree); no dataset directly measures cognitive light cones.

claims.section: The Agent’s Evolutionary Back-Story: Scaling of Information by Bioelectricity
claims.label: Memory and learning are the origin of developmental modularity
claims.claim: Memory can be the beginning of modularity because learning compresses complex states into simple triggers; in somatic control networks this appears as developmental modules in which a single simple driver (e.g. a bioelectric state) initiates a complex morphogenetic cascade such as building an eye or hand.
claims.quote: Importantly, memory can serve as the beginning of modularity because learning essentially groups diverse stimuli into compressed representations: complex states of affairs become remembered as compact biophysical engrams – this is the essence of the kind of modularity when a simple biophysical event kicks off the formation of a complex morphogenetic cascade such as building a “hand” in embryogenesis.
claims.scope: Developmental control networks in animals
measurable_quantities: information content of a triggering signal versus the organ it induces
frequency of single-trigger induction of whole organs (e.g. ectopic eyes)
claims.candidate_data: Published ectopic-organ induction experiments in Xenopus (e.g. bioelectric eye induction) and developmental gene-network models in BioModels.

claims.section: The Agent’s Evolutionary Back-Story: Scaling of Information by Bioelectricity
claims.label: Animal senses use the same ion channel mechanisms found in bacteria
claims.claim: The senses of complex animals (touch, taste, temperature, hearing, etc.) are mediated by the same ion channel mechanisms that bacteria already used to sense their world.
claims.quote: Complex animals’ sense of touch, taste, temperature, hearing, etc. are mediated by the exact same ion channel mechanisms that were already discovered by bacteria and used to make sense of their world (Tasneem et al., 2005; Blackwell, 2006; Liebeskind et al., 2012; Nilius and Honore, 2012).
claims.scope: Sensory ion channels in animals and their bacterial homologues
measurable_quantities: homology of animal sensory channels (mechanosensitive, thermosensitive, voltage-gated) to bacterial channel families
claims.candidate_data: Protein family and phylogeny resources (InterPro, Pfam, UniProt) and structural data in the Protein Data Bank.

claims.section: The Agent’s Evolutionary Back-Story: Scaling of Information by Bioelectricity
claims.label: Cells in development minimize surprise and variational free energy like nervous systems
claims.claim: Living systems minimize surprise and optimize variational free energy by tuning internal states to best predict future stimuli, and this holds for individual cells during metazoan development as much as for nervous systems.
claims.quote: Systems minimize surprise and optimize variational free energy by tuning their internal states in a way that optimally predicts future stimuli (Friston and Ao, 2012; Friston, 2013; Badcock et al., 2019). This is as true for nervous systems as it is for individual cells during metazoan development (Friston et al., 2015; Ramstead et al., 2019).
claims.scope: Nervous systems and individual cells in metazoan development
measurable_quantities: fit of active-inference models to cell signalling and migration time series
prediction error of cellular responses to repeated stimuli
claims.candidate_data: Time-lapse cell signalling and morphogenesis datasets (e.g. the Image Data Resource, Cell Image Library) for fitting free-energy models.

claims.section: The Agent’s Evolutionary Back-Story: Scaling of Information by Bioelectricity
claims.label: Multicellularity and morphological complexity are driven by greedy infotaxis
claims.claim: Morphological complexity and multicellularity are proposed to be driven by greedy infotaxis: cells collecting as much information as possible from as far away in space and time as possible to minimize surprise, with greater network connectivity enlarging what the compound individual can sense, remember and store.
claims.quote: It is proposed that morphological complexity and multicellularity are driven by greedy infotaxis (Vergassola et al., 2007) – collecting as much information as possible, from as far away (in both space and time) as possible, to minimize surprise and optimize prediction.
claims.scope: Origin of multicellularity and morphological complexity
measurable_quantities: information gain of cells in connected versus isolated states
outcomes of simulated or experimental evolution of multicellularity under information-seeking selection
claims.candidate_data: Experimental-evolution studies of multicellularity (e.g. snowflake yeast, Chlamydomonas) and agent-based simulations; no dataset directly tests infotaxis as the driver.

claims.section: The Agent’s Evolutionary Back-Story: Scaling of Information by Bioelectricity
claims.label: Gap-junction coupling lets cells share sensing and form a larger Self
claims.claim: When cells are coupled into networks by gap junctions, the whole collective can measure and act on the same sensory data, so its Umwelt expands into a larger individual; physiological connectivity is thus the binding mechanism for larger unified Selves.
claims.quote: When coupled into networks via gap junctions however, the whole collective can measure and act upon the same sensory data – the Umwelt expands to create a larger individual in which the comprising cells share a unifying picture of the world (Figure 4).
claims.scope: Gap-junction-coupled cell networks in animal tissues
measurable_quantities: spread of a local stimulus response across coupled versus uncoupled tissue
pattern-level outcomes after gap junction blockade
claims.candidate_data: Published gap junction blocker patterning experiments (e.g. planarian and Xenopus studies), and connexin/innexin expression in Xenbase or PlanMine.

claims.section: The Agent’s Evolutionary Back-Story: Scaling of Information by Bioelectricity
claims.label: Most anesthetics in plants and animals are gap junction uncouplers
claims.claim: Most anesthetics that remove cognition and sensory experience, in both plants and animals, act as gap junctional (bioelectric) uncouplers, which the author takes as consistent with connectivity binding cells into larger Selves.
claims.quote: It is thus no coincidence that most anesthetics used to remove cognition and sensory experience, whether in plants or animals, are gap junctional (bioelectric) uncouplers (Mantz et al., 1993; Wentlandt et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2012; Gremiaux et al., 2014; Baluska et al., 2016).
claims.scope: General and volatile anesthetics used in plants and animals
measurable_quantities: fraction of anesthetics that inhibit gap junction conductance at clinical concentrations
claims.candidate_data: Pharmacology databases (ChEMBL, DrugBank, IUPHAR/BPS Guide to Pharmacology) for anesthetic targets and gap junction activity.

claims.section: The Agent’s Evolutionary Back-Story: Scaling of Information by Bioelectricity
claims.label: Swarms should show the same cognitive illusions as vertebrate brains
claims.claim: The proposed scale-invariant scaling of cognition predicts that swarm organisms should fall prey to the same kinds of cognitive illusions and failures of rationality as vertebrate brains, which the author says has been observed in ants and slime molds.
claims.quote: A prediction of this proposed scaling is that swarm organisms should fall prey to the same kinds of cognitive illusions and specific failures of rationality as do vertebrate brains, which has indeed been observed in ants and slime molds (Sakiyama and Gunji, 2013, 2016; Tani et al., 2014; Beekman and Latty, 2015).
claims.scope: Swarm and collective organisms (ants, slime molds) compared with vertebrate brains
measurable_quantities: decoy and context effects in collective choice
susceptibility to visual-illusion analogues in Physarum or ant colonies
claims.candidate_data: Published collective decision-making experiments on ants and Physarum, some deposited in Dryad.

claims.section: Conclusion and Future Outlook
claims.label: Selves form only at intermediate levels of information sharing between subunits
claims.claim: Cognitive light cones grow or shrink as an agent's organization changes, and the key is a balance of selective information sharing through "synapses" (any structures that gate signals based on the state of others): too little sharing fails to bind subunits into a new Self, and too much yields an undifferentiated soup without modules or layered abstraction.
claims.quote: Too little sharing results in a failure to bind subunits into a new Self. Too much sharing results in a homogenous soup with insufficient differentiation of modules and abstraction of information across distinct layers.
claims.scope: Multicellular and multi-agent biological systems
measurable_quantities: degree of gap junctional coupling
degree of tissue differentiation and modularity
coherence of collective behaviour
claims.candidate_data: Network simulations of coupled cells and published gap junction gain- and loss-of-function patterning data; no dedicated dataset known.

claims.section: Conclusion and Future Outlook
claims.label: Cancer is a reversible shrinking of a cell's computational boundary
claims.claim: Cancer is a reversible shrinking of the computational boundary of the Self: by becoming isolated from surrounding tissue's physiological (bioelectric) signals, a cell's cognitive boundary shrinks to its pre-multicellular, single-cell size, so it reverts to proliferating and migrating for its own benefit.
claims.quote: Cancer is a (reversible) shrinking of the computational boundary of a biosystem: by isolating itself from the surrounding tissue’s physiological signals, a cell’s cognitive boundary shrinks to the small size it had before multicellularity.
claims.scope: Carcinogenic transformation in metazoan tissues
measurable_quantities: gap junctional coupling between tumour cells and neighbours
resting membrane potential of transformed versus normal cells
tumour incidence after restoring coupling
claims.candidate_data: Cancer transcriptomic and expression data for gap junction and ion channel genes (e.g. The Cancer Genome Atlas, the Gene Expression Omnibus) and published Xenopus tumour bioelectric experiments.

claims.section: Conclusion and Future Outlook
claims.label: Agents scaled up from homeostatic loops by adding memory, anticipation and networks
claims.claim: Agents evolved by scaling up from basic homeostatic loops (whose set points are the first goals), driven by surprise minimization, through the successive addition of delays (memory), anticipation (inference), and spatially distributed networks that allow learning and abstraction.
claims.quote: Agents scaled up by evolving from basic homeostatic loops, driven by active inference (surprise minimization) via addition of delays (memory), anticipation (inference), and networks (spatially-distributed processing that enables learning and progressive abstraction/generalization from data).
claims.scope: Evolution of agency from early living systems to complex organisms
measurable_quantities: presence of memory and anticipatory signalling circuits in unicellular lineages
phylogenetic ordering of homeostatic, anticipatory and networked control
claims.candidate_data: Systems-biology model repositories (BioModels) of bacterial chemotaxis and anticipatory circuits, plus comparative genomics; no direct dataset for the full sequence.

claims.section: Discussion
claims.label: Morphogenetic goal-directedness smooths the fitness landscape and boosts evolvability
claims.claim: Morphogenetic goal-directedness is a major evolutionary ratchet: because tissues adjust to reach the same anatomical goals despite changed conditions (e.g. muscle, vessels and tendons building a workable extra finger around an ectopic bone), it hides the disruptive effects of random mutations and smooths the anatomical fitness landscape.
claims.quote: Morphogenetic goal-directedness is a major evolutionary ratchet, smoothing the anatomical fitness landscape by hiding the otherwise potentially disruptive effects of random mutations.
claims.scope: Evolution of anatomy in organisms with regulative development
measurable_quantities: phenotypic effect distribution of mutations with and without developmental compensation
evolutionary search speed in models with competent versus passive cells
claims.candidate_data: Mutant phenotype databases (e.g. ZFIN, Xenbase, MGI) and evolutionary simulation studies; no dataset directly measures landscape smoothing.

claims.section: Discussion
claims.label: Brains are not hardwired: ectopic tail eyes in tadpoles still support vision
claims.claim: Brains, like other developing organs, are not hardwired but can ascertain the body's structure and adjust their programs; tadpoles made to develop eyes on their tails, connected to the spinal cord rather than the brain, can still see quite well.
claims.quote: Tadpoles engineered to develop with eyes on their tails instead of in their usual spot can see quite well, despite the fact that the eyes connect to the spinal cord, not the brain (Blackiston and Levin, 2013; Blackiston et al., 2017). Brains, like other developing organs, are not hardwired but are able to ascertain the structure of the body and adjust their functional programs accordingly
claims.scope: Xenopus laevis tadpoles with ectopic eyes; developing nervous systems generally
measurable_quantities: visual learning performance of eyeless tadpoles with ectopic eyes
innervation path of ectopic eyes
claims.candidate_data: The cited Blackiston and Levin behavioural datasets; Xenbase for anatomy and reagents.

claims.section: Discussion
claims.label: Editing bioelectric pattern set points can reprogram anatomy without genome editing
claims.claim: A better strategy for regenerative medicine than genetic rewiring of cells may be to edit the pattern-homeostatic set point and let wild-type cells build to it, as shown by altering bioelectric state in planaria to give permanently double-headed worms without genomic editing.
claims.quote: I have previously suggested that a better strategy than cellular re-wiring at the genetic level may be to edit the pattern-homeostatic set point and let wild-type cells build to the new spec. For example, the ability to re-write target morphology in planarian regeneration was recently shown, by altering the bioelectric state in flatworms, without genomic editing, giving rise to permanently double-headed worms (Durant et al., 2017; Levin et al., 2018).
claims.scope: Regenerative medicine; planarian regeneration as the demonstrating case
measurable_quantities: persistence of double-headed phenotype across rounds of amputation
bioelectric pattern before and after treatment
regenerative outcome of set-point editing versus genetic interventions
claims.candidate_data: Published planarian double-head experiments and planarian genomic and expression resources (PlanMine, SmedGD).

claims.section: Discussion
claims.label: Bioelectric circuits act as software: multistable states switched without genetic change
claims.claim: Ion channel and gap junction circuits are well suited to the "software" of life because they form feedback loops that implement dynamical systems with multiple attractors, which transient signals can switch between without changing the hardware (i.e. without mutating the DNA encoding the channels).
claims.quote: What makes electric circuits, whether ion channel-mediated or electronic, good for software is that they easily implement dynamical systems that have multiple attractors and can be made to occupy one physiological state or another by transient inputs (signals), not requiring changing the hardware (i.e., mutating the DNA encoding that hardware).
claims.scope: Bioelectric networks of ion channels and gap junctions in cells and tissues
measurable_quantities: number of stable membrane-potential states in cell networks
persistence of a bioelectric state after a transient stimulus without transcriptional change
claims.candidate_data: Published bioelectric network models (e.g. BETSE simulations, BioModels) and voltage-dye imaging of tissues.

claims.section: Predictions and Research Program
claims.label: Opiate addictiveness may derive from an ancient role in keeping cells together
claims.claim: If multicellularity arose from a drive to minimize predictive error, cells need a way to keep other cells nearby; this suggests the testable hypothesis that the addictive power of opiates and similar molecules derives from such ancient roots, which could be tested in early models of multicellularity and stem/somatic cell co-cultures.
claims.quote: Specifically, the implementation of multicellularity by the drive to minimize predictive error (Fields and Levin, 2019) suggests that cells need a way to keep other cells nearby. This suggests the testable hypothesis that the addictive power of opiates and similar molecules derives from such ancient roots.
claims.scope: Opioid and addiction-related signalling in early multicellular models and cell co-cultures
measurable_quantities: effect of opioid agonists/antagonists on cell aggregation or co-culture cohesion
phylogenetic distribution of opioid-like signalling
claims.candidate_data: Comparative genomics of opioid receptor families (InterPro, OrthoDB); new aggregation assays would be needed.

claims.section: Predictions and Research Program
claims.label: Forced electrogenic and gap junction expression could make unicells form bodies
claims.claim: The proposed role of bioelectrics in multicellularity predicts that forcing expression of appropriate electrogenic proteins and gap junctions in a unicellular organism should induce metazoan-like bodies, and that appropriate changes of bioelectric dynamics may dissolve a metazoan body.
claims.quote: The proposed crucial role of bioelectrics in multicellularity predicts that it should be possible to induce the formation of metazoan-like bodies in an otherwise unicellular organism by forcing the expression of appropriate electrogenic proteins and gap junctions. Similarly, it may be possible to induce dissolution of an entire metazoan body by appropriate changes of bioelectric dynamics.
claims.scope: Unicellular organisms engineered with electrogenic proteins and gap junctions; metazoan bodies
measurable_quantities: formation of stable multicellular aggregates after transgene expression
coherence of a metazoan body after bioelectric perturbation
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.section: Predictions and Research Program
claims.label: Regeneration across kingdoms should consistently use electrogenic proteins
claims.claim: Bioelectrics should be widely conserved in regeneration across kingdoms: transcriptomes of regeneration from damaged bacterial biofilms to plants to animal limb and organ regeneration should show consistent use of electrogenic proteins, and neurotransmitter signalling should be conserved enough that cognitive-modulator drugs affect biofilms and Physarum.
claims.quote: Bioelectrics should be widely conserved in regeneration across Kingdoms; transcriptomic analyses of regeneration events from damaged bacterial biofilms to plants to metazoan models of limb and organ regeneration should all show consistent use of electrogenic proteins in the events that enable cooperation toward self-limiting morphogenetic cascades.
claims.scope: Regeneration in bacterial biofilms, plants and animals
measurable_quantities: differential expression of ion channel, pump and gap junction genes during regeneration
effects of neuroactive drugs on biofilm and Physarum behaviour
claims.candidate_data: Regeneration transcriptome series in the Gene Expression Omnibus and species resources such as PlanMine and Xenbase.

claims.section: What Does It Feel Like to be a Pancreas?
claims.label: Cells and tissues may have something it is like to make decisions
claims.claim: Because some nervous systems give rise to first-person experience and neural and non-neural networks differ minimally apart from time scale, it is natural to hypothesize that there is something it is like to be a tissue or organ making decisions, e.g. a pancreas may have as much proto-consciousness as a simple neural network.
claims.quote: But, given that at least some nervous systems do give rise to such experience and that the differences between neural networks and non-neural ones (aside from temporal scale) are minimal, it is natural to hypothesize that there is something-it-is-like to being a tissue or organ and making decisions.
claims.scope: Non-neural tissues and organs
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.section: Abstract
claims.label: Evolutionary algorithms can design novel living organisms built from frog cells
claims.claim: A pipeline in which an evolutionary algorithm designs candidate organisms in silico for a desired function, and transferable designs are then built from Xenopus cells with a cell-based construction toolkit, can produce novel living systems that show the predicted behaviours, though some steps still need manual intervention.
claims.quote: Here we show a scalable pipeline for creating functional novel lifeforms: AI methods automatically design diverse candidate lifeforms in silico to perform some desired function, and transferable designs are then created using a cell-based construction toolkit to realize living systems with the predicted behaviors.
claims.scope: Xenopus laevis embryonic epidermal and cardiac progenitor tissue shaped into designed aggregates
measurable_quantities: match between simulated and observed shape
match between simulated and observed locomotion
claims.candidate_data: The paper's source code on GitHub (named in its Data Availability statement) and its SI movement tracks.

claims.section: Results › Locomotion.
claims.label: Designed organisms moved as simulated when upright, much less when inverted
claims.claim: For at least one deciliated, cardiac-muscle-powered design, the upright organisms' direction of movement matched that of the in silico design under random perturbations, and inverting the design significantly reduced net displacement both in silico and in vivo.
claims.quote: More specifically, the upright organisms’ direction of movement matched that of the in silico design under random perturbations (P < 0.01; details in SI Appendix, section S9), and inverting the design significantly reduced its net displacement both in silico (P < 0.001) and in vivo (P < 0.0001).
claims.scope: Deciliated Xenopus reconfigurable organisms with cardiac tissue, compared with their simulated designs
measurable_quantities: direction of movement
net displacement upright versus inverted
claims.candidate_data: The paper's movement tracks (SI) and GitHub code; repeat tracking experiments.

claims.section: Results › Locomotion.
claims.label: Behaviour transfer from simulation to organism was due to the designed shape
claims.claim: The authors interpret the orientation-dependent match between simulated and living organisms as showing that successful transfer of locomotion from simulation to the living organism was due to the designed morphology itself, not chance.
claims.quote: This suggests that successful transference did not result by chance but rather was due to the design itself.
claims.scope: Evolved designs realized as Xenopus reconfigurable organisms
measurable_quantities: locomotion of designed versus random or scrambled shapes built from the same tissues
claims.candidate_data: The paper's SI movement data; control builds of non-evolved shapes would be needed.

claims.section: Results › Object Manipulation.
claims.label: Motile designs spontaneously aggregate particles in simulation and in vivo
claims.claim: When the environment contains particulate matter, motile designs spontaneously gather the particles into aggregates, both in simulation and as living Xenopus-cell organisms.
claims.quote: When the environment is strewn with particulate matter, motile designs spontaneously aggregate the external objects both in silico (SI Appendix, Fig. S10) and in vivo (Fig. 3F and SI Appendix, Fig. S11).
claims.scope: Xenopus reconfigurable organisms and their simulated counterparts in a particle-strewn dish
measurable_quantities: particle cluster size and number over time
claims.candidate_data: The paper's SI videos and GitHub simulation code.

claims.section: Results › Collective Behavior.
claims.label: Pairs of organisms collide, bond and orbit, more so with cilia active
claims.claim: Collective behaviours predicted in simulation were observed in vivo: two organisms often collide, form a temporary mechanical bond and orbit each other for several revolutions before detaching, and this is more pronounced when cilia are not inhibited.
claims.quote: For instance, two designs often collide, form a temporary mechanical bond, and orbit about each other for several revolutions before detaching along tangential trajectories (SI Appendix, Fig. S10). This phenomenon is more pronounced when cilia are not inhibited on the organisms
claims.scope: Multiple Xenopus reconfigurable organisms sharing a dish, with and without cilia
measurable_quantities: frequency and duration of pairwise bonding and orbiting
effect of ciliation on entanglement
claims.candidate_data: The paper's SI videos; new tracking experiments.

claims.section: Discussion
claims.label: Selection for locomotion under random actuation evolved derandomizing shapes
claims.claim: In the voxel-based soft-body simulation with randomly phased contractile cells, selection for locomotion produced morphologies that derandomize motion: shape and the distribution of passive and contractile cells evolved so the global movement was coherent despite random actuation.
claims.quote: As a side effect of selection pressure for locomotion, derandomizing morphologies evolved: evolutionary improvement occurred through changes in overall shape, and distribution of the passive and contractile cells, to collectively derandomize the global movement produced by the random actuation.
claims.scope: Evolutionary design in a soft-body physics simulation of passive and contractile voxels
measurable_quantities: net displacement under random phase offsets
morphological features of evolved designs
claims.candidate_data: The paper's GitHub source code for rerunning the evolutionary simulations.

claims.section: Discussion
claims.label: Cell competence lets neural-less novel aggregates self-organize functionally
claims.claim: The behavioural competence of individual cells and their propensity to cooperate in groups facilitate functional morphogenesis in novel circumstances, so that the designed organisms, despite lacking nervous systems, following novel developmental trajectories and mixing tissues, still possess self-organizing properties that support their designed behaviour.
claims.quote: The behavioral competence of individual cells, and the propensity of cells to cooperate in groups, facilitate functional morphogenesis in novel circumstances. The lifeforms presented here, despite lacking nervous systems, following novel developmental trajectories, and being composed of materials from different tissues, nevertheless possess these self-organizing properties.
claims.scope: Xenopus cells in novel, designed multicellular configurations
measurable_quantities: emergent coordination, repair and collective behaviours not specified in the design
claims.candidate_data: The paper's SI data and later Xenopus synthetic-morphology studies; no dedicated dataset known.

claims.section: Discussion
claims.label: Cardiomyocytes in built organisms spontaneously made phase-matched contractions
claims.claim: Although signalling between cardiomyocytes was not designed or enforced, cardiac muscle cells in the built organisms spontaneously coordinated to produce coherent, phase-matched contractions that aided locomotion.
claims.quote: For instance, although signaling between cardiomyocytes was not enforced, emergent spontaneous coordination among the cardiac muscle cells produced coherent, phase-matched contractions which aided locomotion in the physically realized designs.
claims.scope: Xenopus cardiac progenitor tissue embedded in reconfigurable organisms
measurable_quantities: phase relationship of contractions across the cardiac tissue
displacement per contraction cycle
claims.candidate_data: The paper's SI videos; calcium or voltage imaging in new builds.

claims.section: Discussion
claims.label: Reconfigurable organisms self-repair, closing lacerations
claims.claim: Reconfigurable organisms built from Xenopus cells maintain their externally imposed shape and also self-repair after damage, for example automatically closing lacerations.
claims.quote: Finally, reconfigurable organisms not only self-maintain their externally imposed configuration, but they also self-repair in the face of damage, such as automatically closing lacerations (SI Appendix, Fig. S9).
claims.scope: Xenopus laevis reconfigurable organisms
measurable_quantities: time to wound closure
shape recovery after laceration
claims.candidate_data: The paper's SI imaging; new wounding experiments.

claims.section: Materials and Methods › Evolutionary Design.
claims.label: Adding hydrodynamics and random actuation made simulated gaits match living ones
claims.claim: Designs first evolved on simulated land had bounding gaits that did not transfer to living organisms; adding first-order hydrodynamics and randomized phase offsets produced designs whose behaviour better matched the living systems, in contact with the ground for 93.3% of evaluation versus 52.7% on the first pass.
claims.quote: The behavior of designs generated on the second pass better matched the behavior of the actual living systems: on average, designs were in contact with the ground plane for 93.3% of their evaluation period, compared to just 52.7% on the first pass (SI Appendix, section S6).
claims.scope: Soft-body voxel simulations of Xenopus reconfigurable organisms
measurable_quantities: fraction of gait cycle in ground contact
transfer of locomotion to living builds
claims.candidate_data: The paper's GitHub source code for rerunning both simulation settings.

claims.section: Materials and Methods › Build Filter.
claims.label: Shape concavities of 100 µm or more persist in developing stem cell aggregates
claims.claim: Aggregates of developing Xenopus pluripotent cells tend to close small gaps in their geometry; concavities 100 µm wide or more (12% of body length) gave stable long-term deformations, setting the minimal buildable feature size.
claims.quote: Preliminary work determined that concavities with a width of 100 µm or greater (12% of total body length) produced stable long-term deformations suitable for biological building (SI Appendix, Fig. S7).
claims.scope: Reaggregated Xenopus laevis animal-cap tissue shaped by microsurgery
measurable_quantities: concavity width
persistence of concavity over the organism's lifespan
claims.candidate_data: The paper's SI imaging; new shaping experiments in Xenopus.

claims.section: Introduction
claims.label: All known cognitive agents are collective intelligences made of agential parts
claims.claim: Every known cognitive agent is a collective intelligence: biological agents are made of parts (cells and other components) that are themselves agents in important ways, and there is no truly indivisible cognitive being.
claims.quote: All known cognitive agents are collective intelligences, because we are all made of parts; biological agents in particular are not just structurally modular, but made of parts that are themselves agents in important ways.
claims.scope: All known cognitive agents, especially multicellular organisms
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.section: Cognition: Changing the Subject
claims.label: Memories can persist through complete brain regeneration in planaria
claims.claim: In some organisms such as planaria, memories (prior knowledge and behavioural tendencies) can apparently persist after the complete regeneration of the brain, being transferred onto the newly constructed brain.
claims.quote: Not only that, but memories can apparently persist following the complete regeneration of brains in some organisms (McConnell et al., 1959; Corning, 1966; Shomrat and Levin, 2013) such as planaria, in which prior knowledge and behavioral tendencies are somehow transferred onto a newly-constructed brain.
claims.scope: Planarian flatworms trained before decapitation and head regeneration
measurable_quantities: trained behavioural response in regenerated vs naive worms
latency to perform trained task after regeneration
claims.candidate_data: Published planarian training and regeneration behavioural datasets (e.g. Shomrat and Levin 2013 data) and automated planarian behaviour recordings; none known in a central repository.

claims.section: Cognition: Changing the Subject
claims.label: Tadpoles with eyes on their tails can still perform visual learning
claims.claim: Xenopus tadpoles engineered to have eyes on their tails instead of their heads are still readily able to perform visual learning tasks, illustrating that minds readily adapt to radically altered body architectures.
claims.quote: When tadpoles are created to have eyes on their tails, instead of their heads, they are still readily able to perform visual learning tasks (Blackiston and Levin, 2013; Blackiston et al., 2017).
claims.scope: Xenopus laevis tadpoles with ectopic eyes transplanted to the tail and native eyes removed
measurable_quantities: performance on colour/light visual learning assays
fraction of ectopic-eye tadpoles reaching criterion
innervation of ectopic eye to spinal cord
claims.candidate_data: Published Xenopus behavioural assay data from Blackiston and Levin (2013) and Blackiston et al. (2017); Xenbase for related resources.

claims.section: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: A Proposal for a Framework › Philosophical Foundations of an Approach to Diverse Intelligences
claims.label: Transitions in cognitive capacity are gradual, not binary
claims.claim: Although major differences in cognitive function exist among diverse intelligences, transitions between them have not been shown to be binary or rapid relative to the timescale of individual agents; cognition-related properties form a continuum from humble proto-cognitive systems to advanced minds.
claims.quote: Specifically, while major differences in cognitive function of course exist among diverse intelligences, transitions between them have not been shown to be binary or rapid relative to the timescale of individual agents.
claims.scope: All cognitive systems across evolution, development and bioengineered hybrids
measurable_quantities: distribution of cognitive capacities (e.g. learning types) across phylogeny
onset trajectories of learning capacities during development
claims.candidate_data: Comparative cognition and learning-capacity surveys across taxa; none known as a single dataset.

claims.section: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: A Proposal for a Framework › Philosophical Foundations of an Approach to Diverse Intelligences
claims.label: A system's level of agency must be determined empirically by prediction and control
claims.claim: Under TAME, how much agency a system has is an empirical, observer-dependent question: the correct level of agency to attribute is the one whose model and intervention strategy give the most efficient prediction and control of the system, as established by experiment.
claims.quote: Thus, the correct level of agency with which to treat any system must be determined by experiments that reveal which kind of model and strategy provides the most efficient predictive and control capability over the system.
claims.scope: Any living, engineered or hybrid system
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.section: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: A Proposal for a Framework › Philosophical Foundations of an Approach to Diverse Intelligences
claims.label: Gene regulatory network models exhibit associative learning
claims.claim: Analyses of biological gene regulatory network models show that they exhibit associative and several other kinds of learning, as well as pattern completion and generalization, suggesting GRNs could be trained with patterned stimuli rather than rewired.
claims.quote: Indeed, recent analyses of biological GRN models reveal that they exhibit associative and several other kinds of learning capacity, as well as pattern completion and generalization (Watson et al., 2010, 2014; Szilagyi et al., 2020; Biswas et al., 2021).
claims.scope: Published ODE models of biological gene regulatory networks
measurable_quantities: change in response to a conditioned stimulus after paired stimulation
habituation and sensitization in network outputs
claims.candidate_data: Curated GRN models in BioModels, against which learning protocols can be simulated; transcriptomic time series in the Gene Expression Omnibus for in vivo tests.

claims.section: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: A Proposal for a Framework › Specific Conceptual Components of the Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere Framework
claims.label: A Self is marked by goals, compound memories and credit assignment above its parts
claims.claim: TAME defines the hallmarks of a Self as the ability to pursue goals, to own compound (e.g. associative) memories, and to serve as the locus of credit assignment (reward or punishment), each at a scale larger than any of its components can achieve alone.
claims.quote: The TAME framework takes the following as the basic hallmarks of being a Self: the ability to pursue goals, to own compound (e.g., associative) memories, and to serve as the locus for credit assignment (be rewarded or punished), where all of these are at a scale larger than possible for any of its components alone.
claims.scope: Any agent, biological or engineered
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.section: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: A Proposal for a Framework › Specific Conceptual Components of the Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere Framework
claims.label: The spatiotemporal scale of an agent's goals delineates its Self (cognitive light cone)
claims.claim: Selves can be classified and compared by the spatio-temporal scale of the goals they can represent and work toward (their 'cognitive light cone'), and this scale delineates the boundaries of each Self.
claims.quote: Specifically (Figure 4), a “space-time” diagram can be created where the spatio-temporal scale of any agent’s goals delineates that Self and its cognitive boundaries.
claims.scope: Agents from microbes to humans and engineered systems
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.section: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: A Proposal for a Framework › Specific Conceptual Components of the Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere Framework
claims.label: Stress binds distributed modules into one larger homeostatic loop
claims.claim: Stress, defined as a system-level response to the difference between current state and a setpoint, scales Selves by binding modules that sense and act at different scales and locations into one global homeostatic loop; propagated stress signals recruit distant sub-agents to act so as to reduce their own stress.
claims.quote: Stress is a systemic response to a difference between current state and a desired setpoint; it is an essential component to scaling of Selves because it enables different modules (which sense and act on things at different scales and in distributed locations) to be bound together in one global homeostatic loop (toward a larger purpose).
claims.scope: Multicellular organisms and other multi-scale agents
measurable_quantities: stress-signal levels in tissues near vs far from a perturbation
recruitment of distant cells (migration, proliferation, compensatory hypertrophy) after local damage
claims.candidate_data: Injury-response transcriptomes in the Gene Expression Omnibus; compensatory hypertrophy datasets in published organ-injury studies.

claims.section: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: A Proposal for a Framework › Specific Conceptual Components of the Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere Framework
claims.label: Behavioural problem-solving in 3D space derives from older problem-solving in other spaces
claims.claim: Problem-solving behaviour of animals in three-dimensional space is proposed to be a variant of an evolutionarily more ancient capacity to solve problems in metabolic, physiological, transcriptional and morphogenetic spaces.
claims.quote: It is proposed that the traditional problem-solving behavior we see in standard animals in 3D space is just a variant of evolutionarily more ancient capacity to solve problems in metabolic, physiological, transcriptional, and morphogenetic spaces (as one possible sequential timeline along which evolution pivoted some of the same strategies to solve problems in new spaces).
claims.scope: Evolution of problem-solving capacities across life
measurable_quantities: shared molecular machinery between morphogenetic and behavioural control
phylogenetic order of appearance of these capacities
claims.candidate_data: Comparative genomics (Ensembl, OrthoDB) and Gene Ontology annotations of developmental and behavioural genes.

claims.section: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: A Proposal for a Framework › Specific Conceptual Components of the Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere Framework
claims.label: Planaria regenerate barium-insensitive heads after barium-induced head loss
claims.claim: Planaria exposed to barium, a non-specific potassium channel blocker, lose their heads but soon regenerate heads that are completely insensitive to barium, by transcriptionally regulating relatively few genes; the authors interpret this as cells navigating transcriptional space to solve a novel physiological stressor not met in evolution.
claims.quote: For example, when planaria are exposed to barium, a non-specific potassium channel blocker, their heads explode. Remarkably, they soon regenerate heads that are completely insensitive to barium (Emmons-Bell et al., 2019).
claims.scope: Planarian flatworms chronically exposed to barium chloride
measurable_quantities: head degeneration under barium
barium sensitivity of regenerated heads
number of differentially expressed genes in adapted heads
claims.candidate_data: Planarian RNA-seq data from Emmons-Bell et al. (2019) if deposited in the Gene Expression Omnibus; PlanMine for planarian transcript references.

claims.section: Somatic Cognition: An Example of Unconventional Agency in Detail › Goal-Directed Activity in Morphogenesis
claims.label: Picasso tadpoles with scrambled faces become largely normal frogs
claims.claim: Xenopus tadpoles whose craniofacial organs were placed in abnormal positions ('Picasso tadpoles') tend to become largely normal frogs, because the organs move along novel, abnormal paths and stop at the correct frog-face positions, showing that craniofacial remodelling is goal-directed rather than hardwired.
claims.quote: Amazingly, they tend to turn into largely normal frogs because the craniofacial organs move in novel, abnormal paths [sometimes overshooting and needing to return a bit (Pinet et al., 2019)] and stop when they get to the correct frog face positions.
claims.scope: Xenopus laevis tadpoles with experimentally scrambled craniofacial organs undergoing metamorphosis
measurable_quantities: craniofacial organ positions before and after metamorphosis
trajectories of organ movement
fraction of animals with normal frog face
claims.candidate_data: Published craniofacial morphometry from Vandenberg et al. (2012) and Pinet et al. (2019); Xenbase for staging and anatomy references.

claims.section: Somatic Cognition: An Example of Unconventional Agency in Detail › Pattern Memory: A Key Component of Homeostatic Loops
claims.label: Deer antler trophic memory is a rewritable pattern memory
claims.claim: In deer, a wound made on a branched antler in one year leads to ectopic tines at the same location in later years after the antler is shed, which the author interprets as an experience-dependent, rewritable pattern memory in which the target morphology is rewritten without changing the genome.
claims.quote: This is an example of experience-dependent, re-writable pattern memory, in which the target morphology (the setpoint for anatomical homeostasis) is re-written within standard hardware.
claims.scope: Antlered deer (Cervidae) after antler injury
measurable_quantities: position of ectopic tines in subsequent years relative to prior injury site
persistence of the effect across years
claims.candidate_data: Historical antler injury records (Bubenik) and modern antler morphometry; none known in a public repository.

claims.section: Somatic Cognition: An Example of Unconventional Agency in Detail › Pattern Memory: A Key Component of Homeostatic Loops
claims.label: Altering planarian voltage patterns changes head number and head species-shape
claims.claim: In planaria, manipulating the endogenous bioelectric voltage pattern by targeting gap junctions or ion channels can produce worms with one, two or zero heads, or with head and brain shapes resembling other extant planarian species.
claims.quote: Manipulation of the normal voltage pattern by targeting the gap junctions (Sordillo and Bargmann, 2021) or ion channels can give rise to planaria with one, two, or 0 heads, or heads with shape (and brain shape) resembling other extant species of planaria (Emmons-Bell et al., 2015; Sullivan et al., 2016).
claims.scope: Regenerating planarian fragments (e.g. Dugesia japonica) treated with gap-junction or ion-channel modulators
measurable_quantities: head number per regenerated fragment
head and brain morphology metrics
membrane potential pattern by voltage-sensitive dye
claims.candidate_data: Published planarian regeneration phenotype counts and voltage-dye images (Emmons-Bell et al. 2015; Sullivan et al. 2016); PlanMine and SmedGD for gene references.

claims.section: Somatic Cognition: An Example of Unconventional Agency in Detail › Pattern Memory: A Key Component of Homeostatic Loops
claims.label: Two-headed planarian state persists through further cutting despite wild-type genome
claims.claim: Planaria with abnormal head number induced by transient bioelectric manipulation are permanently altered: when cut into pieces with no further treatment, the pieces continue to regenerate with abnormal head number despite wild-type genetics.
claims.quote: Remarkably, the worms with abnormal head number are permanently altered to this pattern, despite their wild-type genetics: cut into pieces with no further manipulations, the pieces continue to regenerate with abnormal head number (Oviedo et al., 2010; Durant et al., 2017).
claims.scope: Planarians after transient gap-junction blockade (e.g. octanol) and serial amputation
measurable_quantities: head number in successive rounds of regeneration without treatment
genomic sequence of altered worms
claims.candidate_data: Published serial-amputation phenotype data from Oviedo et al. (2010) and Durant et al. (2017); PlanMine for transcript references.

claims.section: Somatic Cognition: An Example of Unconventional Agency in Detail › Pattern Memory: A Key Component of Homeostatic Loops
claims.label: Transient bioelectric states can rewrite false pattern memories in animals
claims.claim: Modulating a transient bioelectric state is a conserved mechanism by which false pattern memories (altered target morphologies) can be written into the genetically specified electrical circuits of a living animal, analogous to incepting false behavioural memories in brains with optogenetics.
claims.quote: Thus, much like the optogenetic techniques used to incept false behavioral memories into brains (Vetere et al., 2019), modulation of transient bioelectric state is a conserved mechanism by which false pattern memories can be re-written into the genetically-specified electrical circuits of a living animal.
claims.scope: Regenerating animals, chiefly planaria
measurable_quantities: stable change in bioelectric prepattern after transient treatment
regenerated anatomy in subsequent rounds
claims.candidate_data: Planarian voltage-imaging and regeneration phenotype data in published studies; none known in a central repository.

claims.section: Somatic Cognition: An Example of Unconventional Agency in Detail › Multi-Scale Competency of Growth and Form
claims.label: Newt kidney tubules keep correct lumen size when cell size changes
claims.claim: Newt kidney tubules normally made of 8 to 10 cells in cross-section are built from fewer cells when cell size is experimentally enlarged, and from a single cell wrapping around itself when cells are made very large, showing that different molecular mechanisms (cell-cell interactions vs cytoskeletal deformation) can be deployed to reach the same anatomical outcome.
claims.quote: Even more remarkable than the scaling of the cell number to unexpected size changes (on an ontogenetic, not evolutionary, timescale) is the fact that if the cells are made really huge, just one cell wraps around itself and still makes a proper lumen (Figure 6D).
claims.scope: Polyploid newt larvae (Fankhauser's experiments)
measurable_quantities: cells per tubule cross-section vs ploidy/cell size
tubule lumen diameter
claims.candidate_data: Fankhauser's 1945 histological measurements; modern polyploid amphibian or zebrafish histology in the Image Data Resource or Cell Image Library if available.

claims.section: Somatic Cognition: An Example of Unconventional Agency in Detail › Specific Parallels Between Morphogenesis and Basal Cognition
claims.label: Injury to one limb can be read out from the opposite limb within 30 seconds
claims.claim: Limbs show mirror-neuron-like and somatotopic responses to injury outside the nervous system: the type and site of damage to one limb can be read out within 30 seconds by imaging the opposite, uninjured limb.
claims.quote: For example, mirror neurons and somatotopic representation are seen in limbs’ response to injury, where the type and site of damage to one limb can be read out within 30 s from imaging the opposite, un-injured limbs (Busse et al., 2018).
claims.scope: Xenopus tadpole limbs (Busse et al., 2018)
measurable_quantities: contralateral limb signalling response after injury
classification accuracy of injury type and site from contralateral imaging
claims.candidate_data: Imaging data from Busse et al. (2018) if deposited; none known in a public repository.

claims.section: Somatic Cognition: An Example of Unconventional Agency in Detail › Not Just Philosophy: Why These Parallels Matter
claims.label: Genes for morphogenesis and for learning and memory should overlap widely
claims.claim: TAME predicts significant and specific overlap between genes involved in morphogenesis and genes in memory and learning categories, beyond the known shared ion channels, connexins and neurotransmitter machinery; it also predicts that memory genes will appear in genetic studies of cancer, regeneration and embryogenesis.
claims.quote: Significant and specific overlap are predicted for genes involved in morphogenesis and cognition (categories of memory and learning).
claims.scope: Gene sets across animals, testable by bioinformatics
measurable_quantities: overlap of Gene Ontology morphogenesis and learning/memory gene sets vs chance
enrichment of memory genes in cancer, regeneration and embryogenesis screens
claims.candidate_data: Gene Ontology annotations, Alliance of Genome Resources, Mouse Genome Informatics phenotype annotations, and regeneration and cancer screens in the Gene Expression Omnibus.

claims.section: Somatic Cognition: An Example of Unconventional Agency in Detail › Not Just Philosophy: Why These Parallels Matter
claims.label: Morphogenesis should be trainable by reinforcement for specific anatomical outcomes
claims.claim: TAME predicts (not yet tested) that the collective intelligence of tissues may be trainable by reinforcement learning, using rewards and punishments such as nutrients, endorphins or shock, to produce specific morphological or gene-expression outcomes.
claims.quote: Another key prediction that remains to be tested (ongoing in our lab) is trainability of morphogenesis. The collective intelligence of tissues could be sophisticated enough to be trainable via reinforcement learning for specific morphological outcomes.
claims.scope: Regenerating or developing animal tissues; clinical settings
measurable_quantities: morphological outcome after paired stimulus-reward training vs controls
persistence of trained outcome
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.section: Somatic Cognition: An Example of Unconventional Agency in Detail › Non-neural Bioelectricity: What Bodies Think About
claims.label: Voltage-sensitive channels and gap junctions form rewritable dynamical memories
claims.claim: Because ion channels and gap junctions are themselves voltage-sensitive, a transient voltage state can trigger progressive depolarization or gap-junction closure, so non-neural bioelectric circuits readily form dynamical-system memories that store information and change computation without changing the channel or junction hardware.
claims.quote: The fact that a transient voltage state passing through a cell can set off a cycle of progressive depolarization (like an action potential) or gap junctional (GJ) closure means that such circuits readily form dynamical systems memories which can store different information and change their computational behavior without changing the hardware
claims.scope: Non-neural cell networks coupled by voltage-gated channels and gap junctions
measurable_quantities: bistability of Vmem after transient perturbation
persistence of voltage states without changes in channel expression
claims.candidate_data: Bioelectric circuit models (e.g. BETSE-based published models) and voltage-imaging datasets; BioModels for related electrophysiology models.

claims.section: Somatic Cognition: An Example of Unconventional Agency in Detail › A Bioelectric Model of the Scaling of the Self
claims.label: Gap junctions merge cells into a larger Self by erasing signal ownership
claims.claim: Because signals passing through gap junctions carry no marker of their cell of origin, gap-junctional coupling partially erases informational (memory) boundaries between cells, which promotes the formation of a larger Self whose parts work toward common goals.
claims.quote: Thus, this property of GJ coupling promotes the creation of a larger Self by partially erasing the mnemic boundaries between the parts which might impair their ability to work toward a common goal.
claims.scope: Gap-junction-coupled cell collectives in metazoan tissues
measurable_quantities: spread of second messengers (e.g. calcium) through coupled cells
coordination of collective cell behaviour with vs without coupling
claims.candidate_data: Calcium-imaging datasets of coupled epithelia (e.g. in the Image Data Resource or Zenodo); connexin knockout phenotypes in Mouse Genome Informatics.

claims.section: Somatic Cognition: An Example of Unconventional Agency in Detail › A Bioelectric Model of the Scaling of the Self
claims.label: Cancer is a shrinking of the Self after gap junction closure
claims.claim: Oncogene expression and carcinogen exposure close gap junctions, and the consequence is transformation to cancer, in which cells revert to unicellular-like selves, shrink their computational boundaries and treat the rest of the body as external environment.
claims.quote: Indeed this occurs in cancer, where oncogene expression and carcinogen exposure leads to a closure of GJs (Vine and Bertram, 2002; Leithe et al., 2006). The consequence of this is transformation to cancer, where cells revert to their ancient unicellular selves (Levin, 2021b)—shrinking their computational boundaries and treating the rest of the body as external environment.
claims.scope: Metazoan cells undergoing oncogenic transformation
measurable_quantities: gap-junctional coupling in tumour vs normal tissue
connexin expression in tumours
tumour incidence after restoring coupling
claims.candidate_data: Connexin expression in The Cancer Genome Atlas and the Human Protein Atlas; tumour transcriptomes in the Gene Expression Omnibus.

claims.section: Somatic Cognition: An Example of Unconventional Agency in Detail › A Bioelectric Model of the Scaling of the Self
claims.label: Managing bioelectric connectivity induces or suppresses cancer independent of genetics
claims.claim: Managing bioelectric connectivity between cells can override genetically determined states, inducing metastatic melanoma in a wild-type background or suppressing tumorigenesis driven by strong oncogenes such as p53 or KRAS mutations, so genetic alterations are not necessary either to induce or to revert cancer.
claims.quote: Indeed, recent data show that managing this connectivity can override default genetically-determined states, inducing metastatic melanoma in a perfectly wild-type background (Blackiston et al., 2011) or suppressing tumorigenesis induced by strong oncogenes like p53 or KRAS mutations (Chernet and Levin, 2013a,b).
claims.scope: Xenopus laevis embryos (melanocyte conversion and oncogene-induced tumour-like structures)
measurable_quantities: melanocyte hyperpigmentation and invasion after depolarization
tumour incidence in oncogene-expressing embryos with hyperpolarization
claims.candidate_data: Published Xenopus data from Blackiston et al. (2011) and Chernet and Levin (2013); Xenbase.

claims.section: Evolutionary Aspects › Somatic Bioelectrics Reveals the Origin of Complex Cognitive Systems
claims.label: Developmental bioelectricity preceded and gave rise to nervous systems
claims.claim: Developmental bioelectrics is an ancient precursor of nervous systems: evolution first used analog bioelectric dynamics to position body configuration in developmental morphospace, long before some cells specialized in fast digital spiking to control behaviour in 3D space.
claims.quote: Evolution first exploited this to enable cell groups to position the body configuration in developmental morphospace, long before some cells specialized to use very fast, digital spiking as neural networks for control of behavior as movement in 3-dimensional space (Fields et al., 2020).
claims.scope: Evolution of bioelectric signalling and nervous systems in animals
measurable_quantities: bioelectric patterning roles in early-branching non-neural animals (e.g. sponges, placozoans)
phylogenetic origin of neural genes vs developmental bioelectric genes
claims.candidate_data: Comparative genomes in Ensembl Metazoa and NCBI; placozoan and sponge single-cell atlases in the Gene Expression Omnibus.

claims.section: Evolutionary Aspects › Somatic Bioelectrics Reveals the Origin of Complex Cognitive Systems
claims.label: Context-sensitive ion channels appear alongside complex metazoan body plans
claims.claim: Ion channel phylogeny is ancient (many channel families likely predate the most recent unicellular ancestor of animals), and the appearance of context-sensitive channels enabling new bioelectric feedback loops tracks the appearance of complex body plans at the emergence of metazoa, indicating an evolutionary continuum from single-cell excitability to cognition via somatic pattern control.
claims.quote: The phylogeny of ion channels is ancient, and the appearance of context-sensitive channels (enabling new kinds of bioelectrical feedback loops) tracks well with the appearance of complex body plans at the emergence of metazoa (Moran et al., 2015), revealing the remarkable evolutionary continuum that leads from membrane excitability in single cells to cognitive functions in advanced organisms, by way of somatic pattern control (Cook et al., 2014).
claims.scope: Ion channel gene families across unicellular eukaryotes and early-branching metazoans
measurable_quantities: presence/absence of voltage- and ligand-gated channel families per lineage
estimated origin times of channel families
body-plan complexity per lineage
claims.candidate_data: Genome and proteome resources (Ensembl, UniProt, NCBI Genome, Pfam/InterPro domain annotations) for choanoflagellates, sponges, ctenophores, cnidarians and bilaterians.

claims.section: Evolutionary Aspects › Somatic Bioelectrics Reveals the Origin of Complex Cognitive Systems
claims.label: A single ion channel can induce complete ectopic eyes where Pax6 cannot
claims.claim: In Xenopus, the action of a single ion channel can induce an eye-specific bioelectric state that creates complete eyes in gut endoderm, spinal cord and posterior tissues, locations where genetic master regulators such as Pax6 are insufficient in vertebrates; bioelectric states thus act as master regulators that evolution can exploit for modular anatomical change.
claims.quote: For example, the action of a single ion channel can induce an eye-specific bioelectric state that creates complete eyes in gut endoderm, spinal cord, and posterior tissues (Pai et al., 2012)—locations where genetic “master regulators” like the Pax6 transcription factor are insufficient in vertebrates (Chow et al., 1999).
claims.scope: Xenopus laevis embryos misexpressing ion channels
measurable_quantities: incidence of ectopic eyes by tissue
membrane potential of induced cells
eye marker expression
claims.candidate_data: Published Xenopus ectopic-eye data from Pai et al. (2012); Xenbase for eye marker expression.

claims.section: Evolutionary Aspects › Somatic Bioelectrics Reveals the Origin of Complex Cognitive Systems
claims.label: Mutations in electrogenic genes can produce coordinated, long-range anatomical change
claims.claim: Because the same membrane-voltage dynamics can be produced by many ion-channel combinations and bioelectric states act across tissue distances, evolution can swap channels freely, and simple mutations in electrogenic genes can cause long-range, highly coordinated changes in anatomy (supported by KCNH8 and a connexin in an evolutionary shift of fish fin morphology).
claims.quote: evolution is free to swap out channels and explore the bioelectrical state space: simple mutations in electrogenic genes can exert very long-range, highly coordinated changes in anatomy.
claims.scope: Animal morphological evolution, e.g. fish fins
measurable_quantities: association of ion channel and connexin variants with morphological divergence
fin or organ size in channel mutants
claims.candidate_data: Zebrafish fin-size mutant phenotypes in ZFIN (e.g. longfin, kcnh2a; another longfin, kcnk5b) and comparative fish transcriptomes in the Gene Expression Omnibus.

claims.section: Evolutionary Aspects › Multi-Scale Autonomy Potentiates the Speed of Evolution
claims.label: Multiscale competency shields mutations from selection and smooths fitness landscapes
claims.claim: In organisms with a multiscale competency architecture, whose modules actively correct toward a target morphology, mutations that would be detrimental in hardwired organisms (e.g. displacing the eye) become neutral, so the architecture shields some of mutations' negative effects from selection and smooths the fitness landscape.
claims.quote: Thus, MCA shields from selection some aspects of mutations’ negative effects (which inevitably are the bulk of random mutations’ consequences).
claims.scope: Evolving multicellular organisms; computational models of evolution with competent cells
measurable_quantities: fitness effect distribution of mutations with vs without developmental compensation
rate of evolutionary search in simulated populations
claims.candidate_data: Mutational effect and deep mutational scanning datasets; simulation studies of competent-cell evolution; none known as a direct test.

claims.section: Evolutionary Aspects › Multi-Scale Autonomy Potentiates the Speed of Evolution
claims.label: Anatomical homeostasis may exist mainly to correct mutation-induced deviations
claims.claim: The primary reason for anatomical homeostasis in regulative development and regeneration may be to correct deviations from target morphology caused by mutations, rather than to repair damage.
claims.quote: The primary reason for the anatomical homeostasis seen in regulative development and regeneration may be for dealing, not with damage, but with deviations from target morphology induced by mutations.
claims.scope: Evolution of regulative development and regeneration in animals
measurable_quantities: correlation of regenerative/regulative capacity with mutational load or genome instability across taxa
developmental buffering of mutant phenotypes
claims.candidate_data: Comparative regeneration-capacity data across taxa and mutant phenotype databases (ZFIN, FlyBase, Mouse Genome Informatics).

claims.section: Consciousness
claims.label: Systems operating in morphogenetic or transcriptional spaces have minimal consciousness
claims.claim: TAME provisionally holds that consciousness comes in degrees and that embodiment includes perception-action systems in any space, implying that systems operating in morphogenetic, transcriptional and other spaces should have some, if very minimal, degree of consciousness.
claims.quote: This implies, counter to many people’s intuitions, that systems that operate in morphogenetic, transcriptional, and other spaces should also have some (if very minimal) degree of consciousness.
claims.scope: Tissues, cell collectives and other non-neural systems
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.section: Consciousness
claims.label: General anesthetics block gap junctions, dissolving the higher-level Self
claims.claim: General anesthetics are gap-junction blockers, and on TAME's account shutting down electrical communication between cells makes the higher-level computational layer (the larger Self) disappear while the cells remain healthy; gap-junction blockers anesthetize organisms ranging from plants and Hydra to humans.
claims.quote: Interestingly, general anesthetics are gap junction blockers (Wentlandt et al., 2006): consistent with the cognitive scaling example above, shutting down electrical communication among the cells leads to a disappearance of the higher-level computational layer while the cellular network is disrupted.
claims.scope: Anesthetized plants, Hydra and animals including humans
measurable_quantities: gap-junction conductance under clinical anesthetic concentrations
correlation of anesthetic potency with gap-junction block
claims.candidate_data: Pharmacology data in ChEMBL and IUPHAR/BPS Guide to Pharmacology for anesthetic action on connexins.

claims.section: Consciousness
claims.label: Briefly gap-junction-blocked planaria make other species' heads, then revert
claims.claim: Planaria briefly treated with a gap-junction blocker regenerate heads shaped like those of other planarian species but eventually remodel back to their correct species-specific target morphology, which the author takes as parallel to the temporary loss and return of the Self under anesthesia.
claims.quote: Interestingly, and in line with the proposed isomorphism between cognition and morphogenesis, gap junction blockade has exactly this effect in regeneration: planaria briefly treated with GJ blocker regenerate heads of other species, but eventually snap out of it and remodel back to their correct target morphology (Emmons-Bell et al., 2015).
claims.scope: Girardia dorotocephala planarian fragments treated with octanol
measurable_quantities: fraction of fragments with heterospecific head shape
time to remodel back to native head shape
claims.candidate_data: Published head-morphology data from Emmons-Bell et al. (2015); PlanMine for species references.

claims.section: Abstract
