claims.section: An evolutionary intelligence ratchet
claims.label: The competency ratchet predicts no planarian mutant strains with abnormal morphology
claims.claim: The competency-ratchet model predicts, and it is the case, that there are no known mutant planarian strains with abnormal morphologies (unlike flies or mice), explains the difficulty of making transgenic planaria, and the only known permanent abnormal planarian lines (two-headed and randomized 1- vs 2-head forms) arose from bioelectric rather than genetic change.
claims.quote: For example, it predicts the confirmed fact that there are no known mutant planarian strains with abnormal morphologies (the way there are for fruit flies, mice, etc.) and explains why the research community has had such a hard time (despite decades of efforts) generating transgenic planaria.
claims.scope: Planarians compared with Drosophila, mice and other model organisms
measurable_quantities: number of heritable morphological mutant strains per model organism
success rate of planarian transgenesis
claims.candidate_data: Strain catalogues such as FlyBase and MGI for comparison; planarian community resources (SmedGD, PlanMine) and published transgenesis attempts.

claims.section: Implications of multiscale competency for the evolutionary process
claims.label: Multiscale competency smooths the fitness landscape and lets search escape local maxima
claims.claim: The multiscale competency architecture smooths the fitness landscape by reducing phenotypic differences between genotypes, letting evolution explore mutations that would otherwise be lethal (e.g. a mutation that displaces the mouth but has another benefit survives because the mouth self-corrects), which makes search more efficient and helps it overcome local maxima.
claims.quote: By smoothing the fitness landscape, MCA makes the search process much more efficient, improving evolvability by enabling the search to overcome local maxima.
claims.scope: Evolution of organisms with regulative development
measurable_quantities: fitness-landscape ruggedness with vs without developmental error correction
evolvability in simulations
claims.candidate_data: Evolutionary simulations with developmental error-correction; Xenopus craniofacial remodelling data from the cited studies.

claims.section: Implications of multiscale competency for the evolutionary process
claims.label: Developmental error-correction makes mutations neutral and builds up cryptic variation
claims.claim: By buffering mutational effects through developmental regulation, the multiscale competency architecture makes neutral many mutations that would be deleterious under a direct genotype-to-phenotype mapping, so they persist as a pool of phenotypically dormant cryptic variation that can later be exploited.
claims.quote: MCA makes many mutations neutral that would be deleterious in a direct genotype → phenotype architecture. Such mutations whose effects are mitigated by developmental regulation are not weeded out; instead, they persist, generating over time a rich pool of diversity that may be phenotypically dormant, but can be exploited in future.
claims.scope: Evolving populations of organisms with regulative development
measurable_quantities: standing cryptic genetic variation
phenotypic variance released when buffering is disrupted
claims.candidate_data: Cryptic-variation release experiments (e.g. Hsp90 inhibition studies); population genomic data such as the Drosophila Genetic Reference Panel.

claims.section: Beyond standard model organisms: stories of plasticity and change
claims.label: Physarum learns and decides without neurons, and its behaviour is its morphological change
claims.claim: The unicellular slime mould Physarum learns from repeated experience and makes decisions (e.g. growing towards the heavier of distant inert objects) without a brain, neurons or cellularization, and in Physarum behaviour is implemented as change of body shape, blurring the distinction between morphological and behavioural problems.
claims.quote: These examples of learning and decision-making occur in the absence of a brain, neurons, or cellularization. From the perspective of evolutionary change across behavioral domains, one interesting thing is that for Physarum, its behavior is its morphological change.
claims.scope: Physarum polycephalum (slime mould)
measurable_quantities: habituation to noxious substances over repeated exposures
growth direction relative to object mass
claims.candidate_data: Published Physarum behavioural datasets (e.g. on Dryad or Zenodo, if deposited by the cited studies).

claims.section: Beyond standard model organisms: stories of plasticity and change
claims.label: Planarian tail fragments regenerate brains that recall trained behaviour
claims.claim: Tail fragments of planarian flatworms trained on specific tasks regenerate into animals that show recall of the trained information, so behavioural memories are apparently imprinted onto the new brain as it forms, linking the information processing that restores body shape with that which preserves past experience.
claims.quote: Tails of worms trained on specific tasks regenerate into animals that show recall of the original information: the behavioral memories are apparently also imprinted onto the new brain as it forms (McConnell et al. 1959; Shomrat and Levin 2013).
claims.scope: Planarian flatworms (McConnell 1959; Shomrat and Levin 2013 with Dugesia japonica)
measurable_quantities: trained-task performance (e.g. latency or savings) of regenerates from trained versus naive worms
claims.candidate_data: Automated planarian behaviour datasets from the cited studies if deposited; otherwise new training experiments.

claims.section: Beyond standard model organisms: stories of plasticity and change
claims.label: Xenopus tadpoles with only a tail eye can see through it
claims.claim: Xenopus laevis tadpoles produced with no primary eyes and a single eye on the tail can see out of the ectopic eye, which can connect to the spinal cord, showing that a frog's cellular hardware can adapt within one generation to a radical reconfiguration of its visual system.
claims.quote: Tadpoles of the frog Xenopus laevis can be produced with no primary eyes, but one eye on their tails; these animals can see out of an ectopic eye, which can connect to the spinal cord (Blackiston and Levin 2013).
claims.scope: Xenopus laevis tadpoles with transplanted ectopic eyes (author's lab, Blackiston and Levin 2013)
measurable_quantities: performance on visual learning assays
innervation of the spinal cord by the ectopic optic nerve
claims.candidate_data: Behavioural data from Blackiston and Levin 2013 if deposited; Xenbase.

claims.section: Bioelectricity: the ancient cognitive glue
claims.label: Bioelectric network information cannot be read from transcript or protein levels
claims.claim: Because ion channels open and close post-translationally, the same channels can yield different voltage states depending on cell history and different channels can yield the same voltage map, the information content of a bioelectric network cannot be read out at the transcriptional or proteomic level and must be studied in living tissue.
claims.quote: As a corollary, the information content of this network cannot be read out at the transcriptional or even proteomic level: channels open and close post-translationally, and the same channels can give rise to different voltage states depending on cells’ history, while diverse channels can give rise to the exact same voltage map.
claims.scope: Bioelectric networks of neural and non-neural cells
measurable_quantities: correlation between ion channel transcript/protein profiles and measured resting potential across cells
claims.candidate_data: Patch-seq datasets pairing electrophysiology with transcriptomes (e.g. Allen Cell Types Database) and voltage imaging paired with single-cell RNA-seq.

claims.section: Bioelectricity: the ancient cognitive glue
claims.label: Bioelectric networks are a cognitive glue that enlarges the cognitive light cone of cells
claims.claim: Bioelectric networks, through their plasticity, multiscale historicity (memory) and learning capacity, act as a 'cognitive glue' that binds the cybernetic goal-directedness of single cells into a higher-order system pursuing larger-scale goals (a larger cognitive light cone), and this capacity is not unique to brains.
claims.quote: Bioelectric networks, with their inherent plasticity, multiscale historicity, and learning capacity, are an ideal kind of “cognitive glue” that binds the primitive goal-directedness (in the cybernetic sense) of single cells into a higher order system with a larger cognitive light cone (Fig. 1E).
claims.scope: Neural and non-neural cell collectives in multicellular organisms
measurable_quantities: effect of disrupting gap-junctional or bioelectric coupling on the spatial scale of coordinated patterning or repair
claims.candidate_data: Gap-junction blocker and connexin mutant phenotype data in model organisms (ZFIN, MGI, Xenbase); no dataset measures goal scale directly.

claims.section: Bioelectricity: the ancient cognitive glue
claims.label: Neural bioelectric machinery was an evolutionary pivot from navigating morphospace
claims.claim: Ion channels, gap junctions and neurotransmitters were originally used to control cell behaviours toward morphogenetic outcomes (navigating anatomical morphospace); their use to drive 3D behaviour via muscle is an evolutionary pivot, exapted with a speed-up from hours to milliseconds and a shift from spatial to temporal (spiking) patterns, and this conservation is why neuroscience tools work throughout the body.
claims.quote: The current use of these components to implement behaviors in 3D space by controlling muscle activity represents an evolutionary pivot: their original usage was to navigate anatomical morphospace (Fields et al. 2020) (that is, to control all cell behaviors toward specific morphogenetic outcomes).
claims.scope: Evolution of animal nervous systems from non-neural bioelectric signalling
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic distribution and developmental roles of ion channel, connexin/innexin and neurotransmitter genes in non-neural lineages
claims.candidate_data: Comparative genomics of ion channel and gap-junction gene families across early-branching animals and unicellular relatives (e.g. Ensembl Metazoa, UniProt).

claims.section: Basal cognition without neurons: what dynamic bodies think about › Memory and target morphology
claims.label: Morphogenetic pattern memory habituates: repeatedly amputated axolotl limbs stop regrowing
claims.claim: The anatomical setpoint that guides regeneration is a pattern memory that is stable but modifiable by experience; for example, repeated amputation of axolotl limbs leads the tissue to habituate to the loss and eventually stop trying to regrow.
claims.quote: This pattern memory can, like any good memory, be modified by experience (it is stable, but also labile to the right kinds of stimuli). For example, repeated amputation of axolotl limbs leads to the tissue habituating to the loss of limb and eventually giving up trying to re-grow (Bryant et al. 2017).
claims.scope: Axolotl (Ambystoma mexicanum) limb regeneration and regenerating animals generally
measurable_quantities: regeneration success versus number of repeated amputations
claims.candidate_data: Repeated-amputation data from Bryant et al. 2017 if deposited; axolotl genomic and transcriptomic resources (e.g. the Axolotl-omics portal).

claims.section: Basal cognition without neurons: what dynamic bodies think about › Memory and target morphology
claims.label: Deer antlers re-form an ectopic branch at a past injury site year after year
claims.claim: In deer trophic memory, an ectopic branch is formed in the otherwise stereotyped antler at the location of earlier damage year after year, long after the damaged rack has been shed, a memory of 3D position held by scalp cells that regenerate the antler annually.
claims.quote: Trophic memory in deer (Bubenik and Pavlansky 1965; Lobo et al. 2014) enables an ectopic branch in their otherwise stereotypical antler structure to be formed year after year, at a specific point of earlier damage, long after the damaged antler rack has been shed
claims.scope: Deer (Cervidae) antler regeneration
measurable_quantities: recurrence of ectopic tines at injury sites across successive antler cycles
claims.candidate_data: Historical antler morphology records (Bubenik and Pavlansky 1965) and the data compiled by Lobo et al. 2014; none known as a deposited dataset.

claims.section: Basal cognition without neurons: what dynamic bodies think about › Re-writing morphogenetic memories: ontogenetic and evolutionary timescales
claims.label: Bioelectrically induced two-headed planaria stay two-headed across later regenerations
claims.claim: In planarian flatworms the number of heads a regenerating fragment builds is set by the state of a bioelectric circuit with a default of one; transiently modifying it re-sets it to 'two', and the resulting two-headed worms keep regenerating as two-headed through multiple rounds of cutting without further manipulation, unless the pattern is experimentally reset.
claims.quote: Remarkably, when cut again in multiple subsequent rounds of regeneration (with no further manipulation), the fragments continue to result in two-headed animals. This shift in the target morphology for regeneration is permanent (unless the animal’s bioelectric pattern memory is reset back to a one-headed state by an experimental manipulation).
claims.scope: Planarian flatworms (Dugesia japonica), author's lab (Oviedo et al. 2010; Durant et al. 2019)
measurable_quantities: fraction of two-headed regenerates across successive amputation rounds
anterior–posterior membrane potential pattern
claims.candidate_data: Planarian resources PlanMine and SmedGD for gene expression; regeneration scoring data from the original studies if deposited.

claims.section: Basal cognition without neurons: what dynamic bodies think about › Re-writing morphogenetic memories: ontogenetic and evolutionary timescales
claims.label: Planarian head number is not directly encoded in the genome
claims.claim: How many heads a planarian cellular collective produces is not directly encoded in its genome, since the same wild-type cells can produce 1-, 2- or 0-headed planaria depending on their history; the genome encodes the hardware (e.g. ion channels) while the outcome results from experience-sensitive electrophysiological 'software'.
claims.quote: The question, of how many heads a given cellular collective will produce, is, surprisingly, not directly encoded in its genome because exactly the same, wild-type set of cells can produce 1-, 2-, or 0-headed planaria depending on their history.
claims.scope: Planarian flatworms
measurable_quantities: genomic differences (if any) between one- and two-headed lines derived from the same wild-type stock
claims.candidate_data: Planarian genome assemblies (SmedGD, PlanMine) and resequencing of two-headed lines if available.

claims.section: Basal cognition without neurons: what dynamic bodies think about › Re-writing morphogenetic memories: ontogenetic and evolutionary timescales
claims.label: Genetic assimilation of bioelectric phenotypes likely shaped body-plan evolution
claims.claim: Evolutionary changes in ion channel properties that lead to genetic assimilation of bioelectrically induced phenotypes are likely an important aspect of the evolution of body plans and other morphological features, analogous to the Baldwin effect for learning.
claims.quote: Evolutionary tweaks of ion channel properties that eventually lead to genetic assimilation of bioelectrically induced phenotypes is likely an important aspect of the evolution of body plans and other morphological features, much as the Baldwin effect is thought to be a key dynamic for the role of cognition and learning in evolutionary lineages (Baldwin 1896).
claims.scope: Evolution of animal body plans
measurable_quantities: association between ion channel sequence or expression divergence and morphological divergence among species
whether bioelectrically induced phenotypes become heritable under selection
claims.candidate_data: Comparative genomics of ion channel genes (Ensembl, UniProt) combined with morphological trait databases; assimilation experiments would need new data.

claims.section: Basal cognition without neurons: what dynamic bodies think about › Reprogrammability, external manipulation, and representation
claims.label: Commensal bacteria can hijack planarian morphogenesis to cause two-headed regeneration
claims.claim: Like parasites that manipulate host neurobehavioural systems, commensal bacteria can override the default planarian morphogenetic control system and cause two-headed regeneration.
claims.quote: the planarian morphogenetic control system too can be hijacked not only by bioengineers (as described above) but also by commensal bacteria which can over-ride the default system and lead to two-headed regeneration (Williams et al. 2020).
claims.scope: Planarian flatworms and their commensal microbiota (Williams et al. 2020)
measurable_quantities: two-headed regeneration rate with altered versus normal microbiome
claims.candidate_data: 16S rRNA microbiome sequencing of planaria in the Sequence Read Archive if deposited by Williams et al. 2020.

claims.section: Basal cognition without neurons: what dynamic bodies think about › Reprogrammability, external manipulation, and representation
claims.label: A latent two-head bioelectric pattern is a counterfactual memory of the future target form
claims.claim: Because a two-headed bioelectric pattern can exist in an anatomically normal one-headed planarian with normal gene expression, the bioelectric pattern is not a readout of current anatomy but a representation of the target morphology to be built if the animal is injured, in effect a counterfactual memory.
claims.quote: In the case of a two-headed pattern in a one-headed host, this means that the bioelectrical pattern is not a read-out of what the anatomy is currently, but rather a representation of what it should be, weeks later, following regeneration if the animal is injured.
claims.scope: Planarian flatworms with altered bioelectric patterns (Durant et al. 2017)
measurable_quantities: membrane potential pattern in intact worms
head number of their regenerates after amputation
claims.candidate_data: Voltage-dye imaging and regeneration outcome data from the original planarian studies if deposited; PlanMine for expression data.

claims.section: Basal cognition without neurons: what dynamic bodies think about › Reprogrammability, external manipulation, and representation
claims.label: Ion channel drugs can make planarian head number flip stochastically at each regeneration
claims.claim: Exposure to ion channel drugs can put the planarian bioelectric circuit into a bistable state in which, at each regeneration, fragments of these 'cryptic' worms randomly regenerate as one-headed or two-headed, analogous to bistability in perceptual systems.
claims.quote: Exposure to ion channel drugs (a physiological experience akin to electrical signals from a retina or other sense organ, not a genetic change) can place the bioelectric circuit into a state in which it cannot decide between two outcomes and flips back and forth stochastically at each regenerative event (recall of target morphology).
claims.scope: Planarian flatworms treated with ion channel or gap-junction drugs (Durant et al. 2017)
measurable_quantities: fraction of one- versus two-headed regenerates over successive cuts of the same lineage
claims.candidate_data: Regeneration scoring data from Durant et al. 2017 if deposited; none known otherwise.

claims.section: Basal cognition without neurons: what dynamic bodies think about › Creative problem-solving by adaptive morphogenesis: plasticity, not just emergent complexity
claims.label: Transient gap-junction blockade makes planarian fragments build heads of other species
claims.claim: Temporary exposure of planarian fragments to a blocker of electrical synapses (gap junctions) causes them to build head shapes of other planarian species 100–150 million years distant, with no genetic change; Levin interprets this as the bioelectric network navigating to other attractors in morphospace, and the worms later remodel back to normal.
claims.quote: One example of this plasticity of morphogenetic behavior (expanding on the default genetically encoded repertoire) is the fact that temporary exposure to a blocker of electrical synapses (i.e., an anesthetic) causes planarian fragments to create the heads of other species, with no genetic change required (Emmons-Bell et al. 2015; Sullivan et al. 2016).
claims.scope: Planarian flatworms (Girardia dorotocephala and related species), author's lab (Emmons-Bell et al. 2015)
measurable_quantities: head shape morphometrics of regenerates after gap-junction blockade compared with other species
time to remodel back to native shape
claims.candidate_data: Head morphometric data from Emmons-Bell et al. 2015 if deposited; planarian phylogenies and species images.

claims.section: Basal cognition without neurons: what dynamic bodies think about › Creative problem-solving by adaptive morphogenesis: plasticity, not just emergent complexity
claims.label: Newt kidney tubules keep normal diameter with fewer, larger cells, down to one cell
claims.claim: In newts whose embryonic cells are made larger (e.g. by polyploidy), kidney tubules use fewer cells to keep the normal tubule diameter and body size, and with enormous cells a single cell bends around itself to form the tubule, showing that different molecular mechanisms are called on to reach the same large-scale anatomical goal.
claims.quote: However, if the cells of the early embryo are artificially made to be larger, fewer cells will be used, resulting in the same (normal) tubule diameter and overall body size. Remarkably, this can be pushed to a fascinating extreme: if the cells are made to be enormous, a single cell will bend around itself, producing the normal size tubule diameter.
claims.scope: Polyploid newt embryos (Fankhauser 1945)
measurable_quantities: cells per tubule cross-section versus ploidy
tubule diameter and body size
claims.candidate_data: Fankhauser's historical histological measurements; new data from polyploid amphibians would be needed.

claims.section: Basal cognition without neurons: what dynamic bodies think about › Creative problem-solving by adaptive morphogenesis: plasticity, not just emergent complexity
claims.label: Xenobots perform kinematic self-replication not known in any other species
claims.claim: Xenobots, proto-organisms that form spontaneously from dissociated frog embryo skin cells, are motile via cilia and perform kinematic self-replication, building copies of themselves from loose cells in the medium, a novel solution reached within 48 h without any evolutionary history of selection as Xenobots.
claims.quote: The most remarkable novel behavior is that of kinematic self-replication: Xenobots build copies of themselves by rearranging loose cells provided to them in the medium. This is Von Neumann-style replication that is not, to our knowledge, used by any other species on Earth.
claims.scope: Xenobots made from Xenopus laevis embryonic ectoderm (Kriegman et al. 2021a)
measurable_quantities: number of offspring aggregates formed per parent
generations of replication sustained
claims.candidate_data: Data and code deposited with the Xenobot self-replication study (Kriegman et al. 2021, PNAS) if available on Zenodo or GitHub.

claims.section: Basal cognition without neurons: what dynamic bodies think about › Navigation: an invariant between morphological, behavioral, and other spaces
claims.label: Scrambled Xenopus tadpole faces reach a normal frog face by new paths
claims.claim: During metamorphosis, Xenopus laevis tadpoles reach the correct frog face configuration not only from a normal tadpole configuration but also from a wide range of experimentally scrambled craniofacial configurations, using new paths through morphospace that end in the same goal region.
claims.quote: For example, during metamorphosis, the tadpole of Xenopus laevis can reach the correct frog face region of morphospace not only from its default starting position (a normal tadpole configuration), but also from a wide range of scrambled configurations (Vandenberg et al. 2012)—using new paths through that morphospace that nevertheless end up in the same goal region (Friston et al. 2015; Pezzulo and Levin 2016).
claims.scope: Xenopus laevis tadpoles with induced craniofacial malformations (author's lab, Vandenberg et al. 2012)
measurable_quantities: craniofacial organ positions before and after metamorphosis
fraction of scrambled tadpoles reaching normal frog face
claims.candidate_data: Craniofacial morphometric data from Vandenberg et al. 2012 if deposited; Xenbase.

claims.section: Basal cognition without neurons: what dynamic bodies think about › Navigation: an invariant between morphological, behavioral, and other spaces
claims.label: A few bioelectrically induced lens cells recruit host cells to build a normal-sized lens
claims.claim: When an ectopic lens is induced in tail tissue by bioelectric modulation, misexpressing the ion channel in only a small subset of the needed cells suffices: these cells recruit unmodified host cells to reach the critical mass for a normal-sized lens, so downstream modules such as size control are activated without micromanagement.
claims.quote: For example, when an ectopic lens (in tail tissue) is induced by bioelectric modulation, it is sufficient to misexpress the channel only in a small subset of the needed cells: once their organ-level goal is specified, these cells will secondarily recruit other (un-modified) host cells as needed to achieve the critical mass needed to produce a normal-sized lens.
claims.scope: Xenopus laevis embryos with ion channel misexpression in tail tissue
measurable_quantities: fraction of lens cells derived from injected (lineage-labelled) versus host cells
lens size versus number of injected cells
claims.candidate_data: Lineage-tracing image data from the original Xenopus ectopic-eye studies if deposited; Xenbase.

claims.section: Basal cognition without neurons: what dynamic bodies think about › E pluribus unum
claims.label: Gap junctions wipe ownership of memory molecules, partly erasing cell individuality
claims.claim: By directly connecting the cytoplasm of neighbouring cells, gap junctions provide an 'owner wiping property' for stress signals and other molecular traces of experience (e.g. calcium flux), so cells cannot tell whether such a signal is their own or a neighbour's; this partly erases individual cell identity and lets the collective scale up measurements, stored goals and actions.
claims.quote: Second, by providing direct connections between the intracellular milieus of cells, they provide an “owner wiping property” for stress signals and other molecular traces of experience: cells cannot tell whether a given memory molecule (e.g., calcium flux) belongs to itself or its neighbors.
claims.scope: Gap-junction-coupled cells in morphogenetic and neural tissues
measurable_quantities: intercellular spread of calcium or other second messengers through gap junctions
coordination of cell responses with and without gap-junction coupling
claims.candidate_data: Calcium-imaging datasets of coupled tissues (e.g. on the Image Data Resource or Zenodo) and connexin mutant phenotypes in MGI and ZFIN.

claims.section: Abstract
claims.label: Single adult human lung cells self-construct into motile multicellular biobots
claims.claim: A single normal human bronchial epithelial cell from adult lung, cultured in extracellular matrix for two weeks and then transferred to a low-viscosity medium, self-constructs into a multicellular, motile spheroid (an Anthrobot) without genetic editing, scaffolds or manual sculpting.
claims.quote: Each Anthrobot begins as a single cell, derived from the adult human lung, and self‐constructs into a multicellular motile biobot after being cultured in extra cellular matrix for 2 weeks and transferred into a minimally viscous habitat.
claims.scope: Normal human bronchial epithelial (NHBE) progenitor cells from adult donors, in vitro
measurable_quantities: fraction of seeded cells forming spheroids
fraction of spheroids that become motile
spheroid diameter
clonality of spheroids
claims.candidate_data: Replication with commercial NHBE cells; the paper's supplementary videos and figures; airway organoid single-cell RNA-seq datasets in the Gene Expression Omnibus.

claims.section: Introduction
claims.label: Morphogenetic plasticity is not restricted to amphibian or embryonic cells
claims.claim: The ability of adult, somatic, genetically wild-type human cells to form a novel functional anatomy with new behaviours shows that the plasticity seen in Xenobots is not restricted to amphibian or embryonic cells, and is a fundamental feature of wild-type cells that needs no direct genetic manipulation to unlock.
claims.quote: The ability of adult, somatic, human cells to form a novel functional anatomy, with unique behaviors, reveals that this plasticity is not restricted to amphibian or embryonic cell properties, and is a fundamental feature of wild‐type cells that requires no direct genetic manipulation to unlock.
claims.scope: Genetically wild-type cells generally, generalized from adult human airway epithelium and Xenopus embryonic cells
measurable_quantities: occurrence of novel self-organized motile morphologies across cell types, species and developmental stages
claims.candidate_data: Published biobot and organoid studies across species and tissues; new attempts with other adult cell types.

claims.section: Results › Human Bronchial Epithelial Cells Self‐Construct into Multicellular Motile Living Architectures
claims.label: Lower viscosity may drive apical-out polarity reversal of airway spheroids
claims.claim: The authors hypothesize that airway spheroids keep cilia in the lumen because basal cells interact with the surrounding high-viscosity matrix, and that moving spheroids to a lower-viscosity, water-based medium may trigger basal cells to migrate inward so the ciliated apical layer takes their place on the spheroid surface.
claims.quote: Given that cilia naturally localize into the lumen due to the basal cells’ interaction with the surrounding high‐viscosity matrix, we hypothesized that changing the culture environment to a lower viscosity level (e.g., water‐based media instead of gel‐based matrix) may trigger the basal layer cells to migrate inward and allow the apical layer to take their place on the spheroid cortex.
claims.scope: Human bronchial epithelial spheroids grown in Matrigel and transferred to low-adhesive liquid culture
measurable_quantities: position of basal-cell markers over time after matrix removal
fraction of surface multiciliated cells
matrix viscosity or stiffness
claims.candidate_data: Live imaging of basal and ciliated cell markers in apical-out airway organoid protocols; published apical-out organoid studies.

claims.section: Results › Human Bronchial Epithelial Cells Self‐Construct into Multicellular Motile Living Architectures
claims.label: Apical-in spheroids become motile within a week in low-adhesive liquid culture
claims.claim: Human bronchial epithelial spheroids that are apical-in and non-motile on release from Matrigel become motile by day 7 in low-adhesive liquid culture, with beating cilia on their outer surface; immunostaining shows a large increase in external multiciliated cells between day 0 and day 7.
claims.quote: This new approach has enabled the originally apical‐in spheroids (that show no motility on day 0 as shown on Figure 1b.1) to became motile by day 7 (Figure 1b.2), featuring highly motile ciliary appendages on the spheroid surface.
claims.scope: NHBE-derived spheroids in vitro, Anthrobot protocol with retinoic acid
measurable_quantities: fraction of motile spheroids at day 0 and day 7
number of surface acetylated-tubulin-positive multiciliated cells
claims.candidate_data: The paper's supplementary videos and immunostaining figures; replication with NHBE cells.

claims.section: Results › Human Bronchial Epithelial Cells Self‐Construct into Multicellular Motile Living Architectures
claims.label: Higher culture viscosity reduces Anthrobot motility and size
claims.claim: Culturing Anthrobots in environments more viscous than the protocol baseline decreases both their motility and their size, suggesting that low-viscosity environments favour the growth of functional, larger bots.
claims.quote: We observed that culture environments with higher viscosity levels than the protocol baseline result in decreased motility (Figure S2, Supporting Information) and size (Figure S3, Supporting Information), suggesting that low‐viscosity environments better facilitate the growth of functional bots as well as yield larger bots.
claims.scope: NHBE-derived Anthrobots in vitro
measurable_quantities: culture medium viscosity
fraction of motile bots
bot diameter
claims.candidate_data: The paper's supplementary figures S2 and S3; replication varying medium viscosity.

claims.section: Results › Human Bronchial Epithelial Cells Self‐Construct into Multicellular Motile Living Architectures
claims.label: Initial cell seeding density is a control knob for Anthrobot size and maturation
claims.claim: Changing the initial seeding density of bronchial epithelial cells in Matrigel (half, default or double 30,000 cells/mL) significantly changes the resulting Anthrobot sizes and the time course of motility, though not linearly, suggesting that seeding density is a tractable control parameter for Anthrobot morphology and function.
claims.quote: These results show that the size and time course of maturation of motile bots could be modulated by altering the concentration of cells in the Anthrobot differentiation culture, suggesting initial cell seeding density to be a tractable control knob for Anthrobot morphology and function.
claims.scope: NHBE-derived Anthrobots in vitro, seeding densities 15,000–60,000 cells/mL
measurable_quantities: seeding density
bot size at dissolution
fraction of displacing movers on days 9–20
claims.candidate_data: The paper's supplementary figures S4 and S5; replication with NHBE cells.

claims.section: Results › Human Bronchial Epithelial Cells Self‐Construct into Multicellular Motile Living Architectures
claims.label: Anthrobot motility onset follows a sigmoidal time course peaking around day 10
claims.claim: After release from the matrix, the number of motile Anthrobots rises along a sigmoidal curve over three weeks, with the largest change in motility on day 10, and this rise reflects a morphological reorganization that exposes cilia on the surface.
claims.quote: To characterize the temporal dynamics of motility initiation, we periodically (every other day) counted the number of motile spheroids for 3 weeks following dissolution and observed a sigmoidal motility profile with peak change in motility on day 10 (Figure 1C).
claims.scope: NHBE-derived Anthrobots in vitro, first 3 weeks after matrix dissolution
measurable_quantities: number of motile spheroids per day
fraction of surface multiciliated cells over time
claims.candidate_data: The paper's Figure 1C data; replication time courses.

claims.section: Results › Human Bronchial Epithelial Cells Self‐Construct into Multicellular Motile Living Architectures
claims.label: Anthrobot motility is cilia-driven
claims.claim: Blocking ciliary motion with ciliobrevin sharply decreases Anthrobot motility, showing that their locomotion is driven by surface cilia.
claims.quote: We administered the efficient blocker of cilia motion, ciliobrevin,[ 20 ] and observed the expected drastic decrease in motility (See Figure S6, Supporting Information), confirming that the motility of Anthrobots is cilia‐driven.
claims.scope: NHBE-derived Anthrobots in vitro
measurable_quantities: fraction of motile bots with and without ciliobrevin
bot speed
claims.candidate_data: The paper's supplementary figure S6; replication with dynein inhibitors.

claims.section: Results › Anthrobots Self‐Organize into Discrete Movement Types
claims.label: Anthrobot trajectories fall into four movement types
claims.claim: Unsupervised clustering of 30-second trajectory segments from about 200 Anthrobots, described by straightness and gyration indices, yields four statistically distinct movement types: circular, linear, curvilinear and eclectic.

gyration index per 30 s segment
cluster membership and proportions

self-transition (persistence) probability per type

inter-type transition rates

polarity index
noise points

claims.section: Discussion

claims.candidate_data: Published left-right perturbation studies; Xenbase and ZFIN laterality-marker expression data.

claims.claim: Single neural crest cells transposed to a different anterior-posterior axial domain change their gene expression to match their neighbours, whereas groups of transposed cells keep their original gene expression, which the authors interpret as collectives having greater positional memory (a perceptual field extending further into the past) than individual cells.

claims.claim: The vertebrate segmentation clock depends on collectivity: presomitic mesoderm cells do not oscillate when cultured individually but resume oscillating when cultured together, wild-type cells grafted into non-cycling mutant fish express her1 without cycling, and cells grafted into tissue at a different clock phase synchronize to their neighbours' phase.
